questions.stem: Adult heights in a town are approximately normal with mean 70 inches and standard deviation 3 inches. Which height is the most unusual?
choices: 79 inches
73 inches
64 inches
67 inches
questions.answer: 79 inches
questions.solution: Compare z-scores: 73 gives 1, 64 gives $-2$, 67 gives $-1$ and 79 gives 3. The value farthest from the mean in standard deviations, 79 inches, is the most unusual.

solve.answer: 79 inches

questions.skill: Normal probabilities from a given area
questions.stem: Test scores are approximately normal. Software reports that the probability of a score below 65 is 0.16 and the probability of a score below 85 is 0.84. What is the probability that a randomly chosen score is between 65 and 85?
questions.solution: The probability below 85 includes the probability below 65, so the probability between them is $0.84 - 0.16 = 0.68$. Adding the two values would give 1.00, and 0.32 is the probability outside the interval.

questions.skill: Expected value of a discrete distribution
questions.stem: The random variable $X$ takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. We know $P(0) = 0.15$, $P(1) = 0.35$ and $P(2) = 0.3$, and the rest of the probability belongs to 3. What is the expected value of $X$?

It costs 3 dollars to play a game with a fair six-sided die. You are paid 12 dollars if you roll a 6, 3 dollars if you roll a 1, and nothing for any other roll. What is the expected net gain per play, in dollars, after paying the 3 dollars?
questions.solution: The expected payment is $\frac{1}{6}(12) + \frac{1}{6}(3) + \frac{4}{6}(0) = \frac{15}{6} = 2.5$ dollars. Subtract the cost: $2.5 - 3 = -0.5$ dollars.

solve.work: Expected payout = 12(1/6) + 3(1/6) + 0(4/6) = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5. Net = 2.5 - 3 = -0.5 dollars per play.

questions.stem: A warranty costs 30 dollars. The item fails with probability 0.1, and a repair costs 200 dollars. Which statement is correct?
choices: On average, the warranty costs 10 dollars more than the repairs it covers
On average, the warranty saves the buyer 10 dollars on the repairs it covers
On average, the warranty saves the buyer 170 dollars on the repairs it covers
On average, the warranty costs exactly the same as the repairs it covers
questions.answer: On average, the warranty costs 10 dollars more than the repairs it covers
questions.solution: The expected repair cost is $0.1 \times 200 = 20$ dollars. The warranty costs 30 dollars, which is $30 - 20 = 10$ dollars more than that on average. A buyer who cares only about the average cost would not buy it.

solve.answer: On average, the warranty costs 10 dollars more than the repairs it covers
solve.work: Expected repair cost = 0.1 x 200 = 20 dollars. Warranty 30 dollars, so on average it costs 30 - 20 = 10 dollars more than the repairs it covers.

questions.stem: Marbles are drawn from a bag one at a time, and each marble is put back before the next draw. Each draw is red with probability $\frac{1}{3}$. In 4 draws, what is the probability of exactly 2 red marbles?
questions.solution: There are 6 ways to choose which 2 of the 4 draws are red. Each such pattern has probability $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{4}{81}$. So the probability is $6 \times \frac{4}{81} = \frac{24}{81} = \frac{8}{27}$.

questions.stem: A player succeeds on each of 5 independent attempts with probability 0.4. Which expression gives the probability of exactly 3 successes?
questions.solution: There are 10 ways to choose which 3 of the 5 attempts succeed (5 choose 3 is 10). Each way has probability $(0.4)^3$ for the successes times $(0.6)^2$ for the 2 failures. So the probability is $10(0.4)^3(0.6)^2$.

solve.work: C(5,3)(0.4)^3(0.6)^2 = 10(0.4)^3(0.6)^2. B swaps exponents (that is 2 successes); A lacks the coefficient; D has the wrong coefficient.

questions.stem: About 95 percent of the values of a normally distributed quantity lie between 40 and 56. Use the empirical rule to find the standard deviation.
questions.solution: About 95 percent of values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so the interval from 40 to 56 spans 4 standard deviations. Its length is $56 - 40 = 16$, so one standard deviation is $16 \div 4 = 4$.

solve.work: About 95% lie within mean -/+ 2 sd. Mean = (40 + 56)/2 = 48; 2 sd = 56 - 48 = 8, so sd = 4.

questions.stem: Commute times in a town are approximately normal with mean 30 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. In a random group of 400 commuters, about how many would you expect to have a commute longer than 40 minutes?
questions.solution: A commute of 40 minutes is 2 standard deviations above the mean. About 95 percent of values are within 2 standard deviations, so about 5 percent are outside, and half of those, 2.5 percent, are above. Then $0.025 \times 400 = 10$ commuters.

solve.work: 40 = 30 + 2(5), z = 2. Empirical rule: about 2.5% above 2 sd. 0.025 x 400 = 10 commuters. (Table 2.28% gives about 9, still closest to 10.)

questions.stem: A bus company claims that 90 percent of its buses arrive on time. In a random sample of 100 arrivals, 78 were on time. If the claim is true, the number on time has mean 90 and standard deviation 3. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: 78 is only 12 below the mean, which is small compared with the sample of 100, so it supports the claim
78 is 4 standard deviations below the mean, which is common if the claim is true, so it supports the claim
78 is 4 standard deviations below the mean, so the claim has been proven false for every single bus
78 is 4 standard deviations below the mean, very unlikely if the claim is true, so it counts against the claim
questions.answer: 78 is 4 standard deviations below the mean, very unlikely if the claim is true, so it counts against the claim
questions.solution: The z-score is $\frac{78 - 90}{3} = -4$. A result 4 standard deviations from the mean is extremely unlikely if the claim is true, so it is good evidence against the claim. It cannot prove anything about every single bus, only that the claim is doubtful.

solve.answer: 78 is 4 standard deviations below the mean, very unlikely if the claim is true, so it counts against the claim
solve.work: z = (78 - 90)/3 = -4. Four sd below is very unlikely if the claim were true, so it is evidence against the claim (not proof). A calls it common; C ignores sd; D overclaims proof for every bus.

questions.stem: The lifetimes of a type of light bulb are approximately normal with mean 1000 hours and standard deviation 50 hours. About what percent of the bulbs last longer than 1050 hours? Use the empirical rule, and answer with the number of percent.
questions.solution: The lifetime 1050 is 1 standard deviation above the mean. About 68 percent of values are within 1 standard deviation, so about 32 percent are outside, and half of that, 16 percent, is above.

solve.work: 1050 is mean + 1 SD. About 68% lie within 1 SD, so 32% lie outside, split equally: 16% above 1050.

questions.stem: Delivery times are approximately normal with mean 40 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes. A delivery counts as on time if it takes 52 minutes or less. Use the empirical rule (68-95-99.7). About what percent of deliveries are on time? Answer with the number of percent.
questions.solution: 52 minutes is 2 standard deviations above the mean, since $40+2\cdot 6=52$. By the empirical rule, 95 percent lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so half of that, 47.5 percent, lies between the mean and 52. Add the 50 percent below the mean: $50+47.5=97.5$ percent.

solve.work: 52 = 40 + 2(6), two standard deviations above the mean. By the empirical rule 95% lie within 2 SD, so 2.5% lie above 52. P(X <= 52) = 100 - 2.5 = 97.5%.

questions.stem: A six-sided die is weighted so that its faces 1 to 6 have probabilities that are proposed in the lists below, in order. Which list is a valid probability distribution?
questions.solution: The probabilities must add to 1. In 64ths, the correct list is $32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 64$, which is 1. The list ending in $\frac{1}{64}$ adds to $\frac{63}{64}$. The list with $\frac{1}{4}$ twice adds to $\frac{95}{64}$, more than 1. The last list adds to $\frac{4}{3}$.

questions.stem: A random variable $X$ takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and $P(X = x) = c(6 - x)$ for each of these values, where $c$ is a constant. What is $c$?
questions.solution: The probabilities are $5c, 4c, 3c, 2c, c$. They must add to 1, so $15c = 1$ and $c = \frac{1}{15}$.

questions.stem: A random variable $X$ takes the values 1, 2, 3 and 4, and $P(X = x) = kx$ for each of them, where $k$ is a constant. What is $P(X \ge 3)$?
questions.solution: The probabilities are $k, 2k, 3k, 4k$ and add to $10k = 1$, so $k = 0.1$. Then $P(X \ge 3) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7$.

questions.skill: Expected value of a discrete distribution
questions.stem: A random variable $X$ takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. We know $P(0) = 0.1$ and $P(1) = 0.4$, and $P(3)$ is 0.1 greater than $P(2)$. What is the expected value of $X$?

questions.skill: Expected value of a discrete distribution
questions.stem: A random variable $X$ takes the values 0, 4 and $a$ with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, and its expected value is 3. What is $a$?
questions.solution: The expected value is $0(0.5) + 4(0.3) + a(0.2) = 1.2 + 0.2a$. Setting this equal to 3 gives $0.2a = 1.8$, so $a = 9$.

questions.stem: A random variable $X$ takes the values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. What is its variance?
Game A pays 10 dollars or 30 dollars, each with probability 0.5. Game B pays 15 dollars or 25 dollars, each with probability 0.5. Which statement is correct?
choices: Game A has the larger expected payout, because its top prize is bigger
Game B has the larger expected payout, because its lowest prize is bigger
Same expected payout and the same standard deviation for both games
Same expected payout, but Game A has the larger standard deviation
questions.answer: Same expected payout, but Game A has the larger standard deviation
questions.solution: Each game has expected payout 20 dollars: $\frac{10 + 30}{2} = \frac{15 + 25}{2} = 20$. Game A's payouts are 10 away from the mean and Game B's are only 5 away, so Game A has the larger standard deviation (10 against 5).

solve.answer: Same expected payout, but Game A has the larger standard deviation
solve.work: Both means 20. SD A = 10, SD B = 5. Same mean, A larger SD.

questions.stem: A carnival game costs 5 dollars to play. A bag holds 2 gold, 3 silver and 5 plain tokens, and you draw one token at random. Gold pays 20 dollars, silver pays 6 dollars and plain pays nothing. What is the expected net gain per play, in dollars, after paying the 5 dollars?
questions.solution: The expected payout is $\frac{2}{10}(20) + \frac{3}{10}(6) + \frac{5}{10}(0) = 4 + 1.8 = 5.8$ dollars. Subtract the 5-dollar cost: $5.8 - 5 = 0.8$.

questions.stem: A game costs 2 dollars to play, and you win with probability $\frac{1}{8}$. If you win, you receive a prize of $p$ dollars, and the 2 dollars is not returned. For what prize $p$, in dollars, is the game fair (expected net gain 0)?
questions.solution: The expected net gain is $\frac{1}{8}p - 2$. Setting it equal to 0 gives $\frac{p}{8} = 2$, so $p = 16$.

solve.work: Net gain p-2 on win (prob 1/8), -2 on loss. E = p/8 - 2 = 0 -> p=16.

questions.stem: A coin that lands heads with probability 0.2 is flipped 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least 2 heads?
questions.solution: Use the complement. No heads: $0.8^4 = 0.4096$. Exactly one head: $4(0.2)(0.8)^3 = 0.4096$. So $P(\text{at least 2}) = 1 - 0.4096 - 0.4096 = 0.1808$.

questions.stem: A quiz taker answers each question correctly with probability 0.6, independently. What is the probability of exactly 3 correct answers out of 5 questions?
questions.solution: There are $C(5, 3) = 10$ ways to choose the correct answers. Each has probability $(0.6)^3(0.4)^2 = 0.216 \times 0.16 = 0.03456$. So the probability is $10 \times 0.03456 = 0.3456$. Forgetting the 10 gives 0.03456, and swapping 0.6 and 0.4 gives 0.2304.

questions.stem: Each of 2 independent trials succeeds with the same probability $p$. The probability that both trials fail is 0.09. What is $p$?
questions.solution: Each trial fails with probability $1 - p$, so both fail with probability $(1 - p)^2 = 0.09$. Then $1 - p = 0.3$ and $p = 0.7$.

questions.skill: Mean and standard deviation of a binomial
questions.stem: The number of successes in $n$ independent trials, each with success probability 0.4, has a mean of 18. What is $n$?
questions.solution: The mean is $np = 0.4n = 18$, so $n = \frac{18}{0.4} = 45$.

questions.skill: Mean and standard deviation of a binomial
questions.stem: A binomial random variable has mean 12 and variance 7.2. How many trials does it have?
questions.solution: The mean is $np = 12$ and the variance is $np(1-p) = 7.2$. Dividing, $1 - p = \frac{7.2}{12} = 0.6$, so $p = 0.4$. Then $n = \frac{12}{0.4} = 30$.

questions.stem: A data set has mean 52 and median 47. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The data are probably skewed right, so a normal model fits poorly
The data are probably skewed left, so a normal model fits poorly
The data are normal, because the mean and median are close
The standard deviation of the data must be exactly 5
questions.answer: The data are probably skewed right, so a normal model fits poorly
questions.solution: In a normal distribution the mean and median are equal. Here the mean is well above the median, which happens when a long tail of large values pulls the mean up: the data are skewed right. Nothing in the information fixes the standard deviation.

solve.answer: The data are probably skewed right, so a normal model fits poorly
solve.work: Mean > median suggests right skew; normal model fits poorly.

questions.stem: In one data set, the value 41 has a z-score of $-0.5$ and the value 53 has a z-score of 1. What is the mean of the data?
questions.solution: The two values are $53 - 41 = 12$ apart, and their z-scores are $1 - (-0.5) = 1.5$ apart, so one standard deviation is $\frac{12}{1.5} = 8$. The value 53 is 1 standard deviation above the mean, so the mean is $53 - 8 = 45$. (Check: 41 is half a standard deviation, 4, below 45.)

questions.stem: The scores of 1000 students on a test are approximately normal with mean 500 and standard deviation 50. Use the empirical rule: about how many of the students scored between 400 and 550?
questions.solution: 400 is 2 standard deviations below the mean and 550 is 1 above. The empirical rule gives about $47.5\% + 34\% = 81.5\%$ of the students in this range. Then $0.815 \times 1000 = 815$.

questions.stem: The daily output of a machine, in units, is approximately normal with mean 100. About 16 percent of the days have an output above 115. Use the empirical rule to find the standard deviation.
questions.solution: About 68 percent of values are within 1 standard deviation of the mean, so 32 percent are outside, and half of those, 16 percent, are above. So 115 is 1 standard deviation above the mean: $\sigma = 115 - 100 = 15$.

solve.work: 16 percent above means 115 is +1 SD: sd = 15.

questions.stem: A die is claimed to be fair. It is rolled 3 times and shows a six every time. If the die is fair, the probability of three sixes is $\frac{1}{216}$, about 0.5 percent. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: It is very unlikely with a fair die, so it proves that the die must be loaded
It is very unlikely with a fair die, so it is evidence against fairness, though not proof
It is very likely with a fair die, so it is good evidence that the die is fair
It is possible with a fair die, so it gives no evidence against fairness at all
questions.answer: It is very unlikely with a fair die, so it is evidence against fairness, though not proof
questions.solution: A result with probability about 0.5 percent under the claim is good evidence against the claim. It is not proof, because even a fair die gives three sixes once in 216 tries.

solve.answer: It is very unlikely with a fair die, so it is evidence against fairness, though not proof
solve.work: Probability 1/216 is very small: evidence against fairness, not proof.

questions.stem: A machine is claimed to make a defective part with probability 0.05, independently for each part. An inspector checks 3 parts and finds at least one defective. If the claim is true, what is the probability of finding at least one defective part among 3 parts?
questions.solution: Use the complement: none defective has probability $0.95^3 = 0.857375$. So at least one defective has probability $1 - 0.857375 = 0.142625$, about 14 percent, which is not unusual enough to doubt the claim.

questions.skill: Normal probabilities from a given area
questions.stem: For the standard normal distribution, a table gives the probability of a z-score below $-1.5$ as 0.0668 and the probability of a z-score below 2 as 0.9772. What is the probability of a z-score between $-1.5$ and 2?
questions.solution: Subtract the area to the left of $-1.5$ from the area to the left of 2: $0.9772 - 0.0668 = 0.9104$.

questions.skill: Normal probabilities from a given area
questions.stem: A scholarship goes to students whose scores are in the top 10 percent. Scores are approximately normal with mean 70 and standard deviation 8, and a table shows that a z-score of 1.28 has 90 percent of the area to its left. What is the lowest score, to the nearest hundredth, that is in the top 10 percent?
questions.solution: The top 10 percent starts at a z-score of 1.28. The score is $70 + 1.28(8) = 70 + 10.24 = 80.24$.

questions.stem: A player makes each free throw with probability 0.6, independently of the others. In 4 free throws, what is the probability that she makes at least 3? Give a decimal.
questions.solution: At least 3 means exactly 3 or exactly 4. Exactly 3: 4 x 0.6^3 x 0.4 = 4 x 0.216 x 0.4 = 0.3456. Exactly 4: 0.6^4 = 0.1296. The total is 0.3456 + 0.1296 = 0.4752.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for the height h, in meters, of a ball t seconds after it is thrown is $h = -5t^2 + 20t + 1$. What height does the model predict at $t = 2$?
An exponential regression model for the number of users y, in thousands, x years after a launch is $y = 40(1.5)^x$. What does the model predict at $x = 2$, in thousands of users?
questions.solution: Substitute $x = 2$: $y = 40 \times 1.5^2 = 40 \times 2.25 = 90$ thousand users.

questions.stem: A regression model predicts a value of 52 and the actual value is 47. What is the residual, using residual = actual value minus predicted value?
questions.solution: Residual = actual minus predicted $= 47 - 52 = -5$. The negative sign means the actual value is below the prediction.

solve.work: Residual = 47 - 52 = -5.

questions.stem: A regression model has $r^2 = 0.81$. What does this tell you?
choices: 81 percent of the data points lie exactly on the curve
The model's predictions are correct 81 percent of the time
About 81 percent of the variation in y is explained by the model
The value of y increases by 0.81 each time x increases by 1
questions.answer: About 81 percent of the variation in y is explained by the model
questions.solution: The value r squared is the fraction of the variation in y that the model accounts for. Here that is 0.81, or 81 percent. It does not mean that 81 percent of the points sit on the curve or that 81 percent of predictions are exactly right.

solve.answer: About 81 percent of the variation in y is explained by the model
solve.work: r^2 is the proportion of the variation in y explained by the model: about 81 percent.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: In a scatterplot, y increases, and the increases get larger and larger: each time x goes up by 1, y roughly doubles. Which regression model fits this pattern best?
choices: Exponential
Linear
Logarithmic
Quadratic
questions.answer: Exponential
questions.solution: Doubling each time x goes up by 1 means y is multiplied by about the same factor (2) at every step. That is the pattern of an exponential model. A linear model adds the same amount each step, and a logarithmic model grows more and more slowly.

solve.answer: Exponential
solve.work: y roughly doubling for each unit increase in x means a constant growth factor: exponential.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A residual plot for a regression model shows points scattered randomly above and below zero, with no pattern. What does this suggest?
choices: The model is a poor fit and another type should be tried
There is no relationship at all between x and y
The model must contain a calculation error
The type of model is appropriate for the data
questions.answer: The type of model is appropriate for the data
questions.solution: A good model leaves residuals that look like random scatter around zero. A curve or other pattern in the residuals would show that the model missed some structure in the data. Random scatter means no obvious structure was missed.

solve.answer: The type of model is appropriate for the data
solve.work: Random residual scatter with no pattern suggests the model type is appropriate.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $y = 200(0.9)^x$. What does the 0.9 tell you?
choices: Each time x increases by 1, y decreases by 0.9
Each time x increases by 1, y decreases by 10 percent
Each time x increases by 1, y decreases by 90 percent
The model predicts that y is 0.9 when x is 0
questions.answer: Each time x increases by 1, y decreases by 10 percent
questions.solution: The factor 0.9 means y is multiplied by 0.9 each time x goes up by 1. Keeping 90 percent of the value is a decrease of 10 percent. The starting value, at $x = 0$, is 200.

solve.answer: Each time x increases by 1, y decreases by 10 percent
solve.work: Factor 0.9 per unit of x: y keeps 90 percent, so it decreases by 10 percent each time x increases by 1. y(0) = 200.

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 4 + 2 \cdot \text{ln}(x)$. What does it predict at $x = 1$? (Use $\text{ln}(1) = 0$.)
questions.solution: Substitute $x = 1$: $y = 4 + 2 \cdot 0 = 4$.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A lemonade stand records its daily profit at different prices. As the price goes up, the profit rises, reaches a highest point, and then falls. Which regression model fits this pattern best?
choices: Linear
Exponential
Quadratic
Logarithmic
questions.answer: Quadratic
questions.solution: A parabola that opens downward rises to a highest point and then falls, which matches the pattern. A line, an exponential function and a logarithmic function never turn around from rising to falling.

solve.answer: Quadratic
solve.work: Rises to a maximum then falls: a downward-opening parabola, quadratic.

questions.stem: Four regression models are fit to the same data. Which has the best fit, judged by r squared?
choices: The model with $r^2 = 0.97$
The model with $r^2 = 0.35$
The model with $r^2 = 0.62$
The model with $r^2 = 0.80$
questions.answer: The model with $r^2 = 0.97$
questions.solution: A larger r squared means the model explains more of the variation in y. Of the four values, 0.97 is the largest, so that model fits best.

solve.answer: The model with $r^2 = 0.97$
solve.work: The largest r^2 (closest to 1) indicates the best fit: 0.97.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for the temperature $T$, in degrees Celsius, $t$ hours after 6 a.m. is $T = -0.5t^2 + 6t + 10$. What temperature does the model predict at $t = 4$?
A cubic regression model for the number of visitors $y$, in hundreds, to a fair on day $x$ is $y = x^3 - 2x$. How many hundreds of visitors does the model predict on day $x = 3$?
questions.solution: Substitute $x = 3$: $27 - 6 = 21$.

questions.stem: An exponential regression model for the number of bacteria $y$ in a dish, $x$ hours after the start, is $y = 100(2)^x$. How many bacteria does the model predict at $x = 3$?
An exponential regression model for a town's population is $P = 500(1.1)^t$, where $t$ is the number of years since 2020. What population does the model predict for $t = 2$?

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 5 + 4\log_{10}(x)$. What does it predict at $x = 100$? (Use $\log_{10}(100) = 2$.)
questions.solution: Substitute: $5 + 4(2) = 13$.

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 10 + 5\log_2(x)$. What does it predict at $x = 8$? (Use $\log_2(8) = 3$.)
questions.solution: Substitute: $10 + 5(3) = 25$.

questions.stem: A regression model predicts that a house will sell for 250 thousand dollars. It sells for 262 thousand dollars. What is the residual, in thousands of dollars, using residual = actual value minus predicted value?
questions.solution: Residual = actual - predicted = $262 - 250 = 12$ thousand dollars.

questions.stem: With residual = actual value minus predicted value, a data point has a positive residual. What does this mean?
choices: The actual value is below the value the model predicts
The actual value is exactly equal to the value the model predicts
The actual value is above the value the model predicts
The model is a good fit for the data
questions.answer: The actual value is above the value the model predicts
questions.solution: A positive residual means actual $-$ predicted $> 0$, so the actual value is greater than the prediction.

solve.answer: The actual value is above the value the model predicts
solve.work: Positive residual: actual > predicted.

questions.stem: At a data point, the actual value is 21 and the residual is $-4$, where residual = actual value minus predicted value. What is the predicted value?
questions.solution: Residual = actual $-$ predicted, so predicted = actual $-$ residual $= 21 - (-4) = 25$.

solve.work: 21 - pred = -4 -> pred = 25.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: Which description of a residual plot suggests that the model is appropriate for the data?
choices: The residuals form a clear curve, rising and then falling
The residuals are all positive, for every value of $x$
The residuals get steadily larger as $x$ increases
The residuals scatter randomly above and below zero, with no pattern
questions.answer: The residuals scatter randomly above and below zero, with no pattern
questions.solution: A good model leaves only random errors, so its residuals scatter with no pattern around zero. A curve, a one-sided set of residuals or a steady trend each show that the model is missing something.

solve.answer: The residuals scatter randomly above and below zero, with no pattern
solve.work: Random scatter about zero indicates an appropriate model.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: At a data point, the residual is 0. What does this mean?
choices: The point is an outlier
The point lies exactly on the curve of the model
The model is wrong at that point by 1 unit
The actual value at that point is 0
questions.answer: The point lies exactly on the curve of the model
questions.solution: Residual = actual $-$ predicted. A residual of 0 means the actual value equals the predicted value, so the point lies on the model's curve.

solve.answer: The point lies exactly on the curve of the model
solve.work: Residual 0: actual equals predicted, point on the curve.

questions.stem: A linear model has $r = -0.95$. What does this tell you?
choices: There is a weak negative linear relationship, since the value is below 1
There is a strong positive linear relationship, since 0.95 is close to 1
There is a strong negative linear relationship: $y$ tends to decrease as $x$ increases
Only 5 percent of the points lie on the line, since $1 - 0.95 = 0.05$
questions.answer: There is a strong negative linear relationship: $y$ tends to decrease as $x$ increases
questions.solution: The sign of $r$ gives the direction (negative: $y$ falls as $x$ rises) and its distance from 0 gives the strength. A value of $-0.95$ is close to $-1$, so the relationship is strong and negative.

solve.answer: There is a strong negative linear relationship: $y$ tends to decrease as $x$ increases
solve.work: r=-0.95: strong negative linear relationship.

questions.stem: A linear model has $r = 0.6$. What percent of the variation in $y$ is explained by the model?
questions.solution: The percent explained is $r^2 = 0.6^2 = 0.36$, or 36 percent.

solve.work: r^2=0.36 -> 36 percent.

questions.stem: A regression model has $r^2 = 0.40$. What percent of the variation in $y$ is NOT explained by the model?
questions.solution: The model explains 40 percent of the variation, so $100 - 40 = 60$ percent is not explained.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: The number of people who have heard a rumor roughly triples every hour. Which regression model fits this pattern best?
choices: Linear
Quadratic
Exponential
Logarithmic
questions.answer: Exponential
questions.solution: A quantity that is multiplied by the same factor in equal time steps is modeled by an exponential function.

solve.answer: Exponential
solve.work: Tripling each hour is a constant factor: exponential.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A student's quiz scores improve a lot during the first few hours of studying, then improve by smaller and smaller amounts, and never decrease. Which regression model fits this pattern best?
choices: Exponential growth
Logarithmic
Quadratic opening downward
Linear
questions.answer: Logarithmic
questions.solution: Large early gains that keep shrinking while the values still rise are the shape of a logarithmic function. A downward-opening quadratic would eventually fall.

solve.answer: Logarithmic
solve.work: Fast gains then smaller and smaller, never decreasing: logarithmic.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $y = 50(1.2)^x$. What does the 1.2 tell you?
choices: Each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ increases by 20 percent
Each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ increases by 1.2
Each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ increases by 120 percent
Each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ is multiplied by 20
questions.answer: Each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ increases by 20 percent
questions.solution: The base 1.2 is the factor by which $y$ is multiplied each step. Multiplying by 1.2 is an increase of 0.2, or 20 percent.

solve.answer: Each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ increases by 20 percent
solve.work: Factor 1.2 means a 20 percent increase per unit of x.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $y = 500(0.7)^x$. By what percent does the model decrease $y$ each time $x$ increases by 1?
questions.solution: Each step multiplies $y$ by 0.7, so $y$ keeps 70 percent of its value and loses $100 - 70 = 30$ percent.

solve.work: 1-0.7=0.3 -> 30 percent decrease.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: The amount of a medicine in a patient's body decays by 12 percent each hour, according to an exponential model $y = a \cdot b^x$. What is the value of $b$?
questions.solution: Losing 12 percent each hour leaves 88 percent, so the multiplier per hour is $b = 1 - 0.12 = 0.88$.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: In a school, students who spend more hours on a tutoring app have higher test scores, with $r = 0.8$. Which conclusion is supported by this data alone?
choices: Hours and scores are associated, but the data alone do not show cause
The app causes higher scores, because the correlation is strong
Spending fewer hours on the app causes higher scores
There is no relationship between app hours and scores, since $r$ is not 1
questions.answer: Hours and scores are associated, but the data alone do not show cause
questions.solution: A strong correlation shows association. Without a designed experiment, other factors (such as motivation) could explain the pattern, so causation is not established.

solve.answer: Hours and scores are associated, but the data alone do not show cause
solve.work: Correlation shows association, not causation.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: A regression model was fit to data with $x$ between 10 and 50, and it is used to predict at $x = 500$. What is the main concern?
choices: The model cannot accept a number as large as 500 as an input
Predictions are reliable only at multiples of 10, because the data start at 10
Predictions are reliable only at the mean of the $x$-values, not elsewhere
The value 500 is far outside the data, so the prediction is an unreliable extrapolation
questions.answer: The value 500 is far outside the data, so the prediction is an unreliable extrapolation
questions.solution: The model describes the relationship only where there is data. Far outside that range, the pattern may change, so the prediction is an extrapolation and may be unreliable.

solve.answer: The value 500 is far outside the data, so the prediction is an unreliable extrapolation
solve.work: 500 is far outside 10-50: extrapolation is unreliable.

questions.skill: Use a model with two or more predictors
questions.stem: A model predicts an exam score as $S = 40 + 2h + 0.5p$, where $h$ is the hours studied and $p$ is the number of practice tests taken. What score does it predict for $h = 5$ and $p = 6$?

questions.skill: Use a model with two or more predictors
questions.stem: In the model $S = 40 + 2h + 0.5p$ for an exam score $S$, with $h$ the hours studied and $p$ the number of practice tests, what does the 2 tell you?
choices: With $p$ held fixed, each extra hour of study adds 2 to the predicted score
Each extra hour of study adds 2 to the predicted score only for students who take no practice tests
Each practice test adds 2 to the predicted score
A student who studies for 2 hours is predicted to score 40
questions.answer: With $p$ held fixed, each extra hour of study adds 2 to the predicted score
questions.solution: In a model with several predictors, a coefficient tells the change in the prediction for a one-unit increase in that predictor while the other predictors are held fixed.

solve.answer: With $p$ held fixed, each extra hour of study adds 2 to the predicted score
solve.work: Coefficient of h: with p fixed, each extra hour adds 2.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for profit P, in dollars, from selling x gadgets is $P = -2x^2 + 12x + 5$. What is the greatest profit the model predicts, in dollars?
questions.solution: The parabola opens downward, so its highest point is at $x = -\frac{12}{2(-2)} = 3$. Then $P = -2(9) + 12(3) + 5 = -18 + 36 + 5 = 23$ dollars.

questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $y = 5 \cdot 2^x$. For what value of x does the model predict $y = 80$?
A cubic regression model is $y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1$. What does the model predict at $x = 4$?

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: For a regression model, the residual at $x = 10$ is $-12$, where residual = actual value minus predicted value. What does this mean?
choices: The actual value at $x = 10$ is 12 above the value the model predicts
The model predicts a value of $-12$ at $x = 10$
The actual value at $x = 10$ is 12 percent below the prediction
The actual value at $x = 10$ is 12 below the value the model predicts
questions.answer: The actual value at $x = 10$ is 12 below the value the model predicts
questions.solution: Actual minus predicted equals $-12$, so the actual value is 12 less than the predicted one. A residual is measured in the same units as y, not as a percent.

solve.answer: The actual value at $x = 10$ is 12 below the value the model predicts
solve.work: actual - predicted = -12 means actual = predicted - 12: 12 below the prediction.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A student fits a straight line to data. The residual plot is U-shaped: the residuals are positive for small x, negative for middle values of x, and positive for large x. What does this suggest?
choices: The line is a good fit, because the residuals add up to zero
A curved model, such as a quadratic, would fit the data better
The data contain errors that should be removed
The value of r must be exactly 1 for this data
questions.answer: A curved model, such as a quadratic, would fit the data better
questions.solution: A pattern in the residuals shows that the model type is missing something. A U shape means the data bend in a way a line cannot follow, so a curve such as a quadratic should be tried. A random scatter, not a pattern, is what a good fit leaves behind.

solve.answer: A curved model, such as a quadratic, would fit the data better
solve.work: A U-shaped residual pattern shows curvature the line misses; a curved model such as a quadratic would fit better.

questions.stem: For the same data, a linear model has $r^2 = 0.62$ and a quadratic model has $r^2 = 0.97$. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The linear model fits better, because a smaller r squared means smaller errors
The two models fit equally well, because both values of r squared are positive
The quadratic model explains more of the variation in y, so it fits this data better
The linear model explains 97 percent of the variation and the quadratic 62 percent
questions.answer: The quadratic model explains more of the variation in y, so it fits this data better
questions.solution: A larger r squared means more of the variation in y is explained. The quadratic explains 97 percent and the linear only 62 percent, so the quadratic fits this data better.

solve.answer: The quadratic model explains more of the variation in y, so it fits this data better
solve.work: The quadratic explains 97 percent of the variation in y versus 62 percent for the linear, so the quadratic fits better.

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 10 + 3 \cdot \text{ln}(x)$ for $x > 0$. Which statement describes how y changes as x increases?
choices: y keeps increasing, but more and more slowly
y increases by exactly 3 each time x increases by 1
y increases faster and faster
y levels off at 10 and never goes higher
questions.answer: y keeps increasing, but more and more slowly
questions.solution: A logarithmic function with a positive coefficient keeps rising as x grows, with smaller and smaller gains. It does not rise by a fixed amount (that would be linear), it does not speed up (that would be exponential), and it has no upper limit that it levels off at.

solve.answer: y keeps increasing, but more and more slowly
solve.work: y = 10 + 3 ln x is increasing (derivative 3/x > 0) and its rate falls as x grows, with no upper bound: keeps increasing, more and more slowly.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $y = 120(1.08)^x$. By what percent does the model increase y each time x increases by 1?
questions.solution: Each time x goes up by 1, y is multiplied by 1.08. That is the old value plus 0.08 of it, an increase of 8 percent.

solve.work: Factor 1.08 = 1 + 0.08: an 8 percent increase per unit of x.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: An exponential model $y = a \cdot b^x$ predicts $y = 6$ at $x = 0$ and $y = 48$ at $x = 3$. What is the value of b?

solve.work: a = 6 (value at x = 0). 6 b^3 = 48 gives b^3 = 8, b = 2.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for a plant's height, in centimeters, was fit to data from weeks 1 through 6 and has $r^2 = 0.98$. It predicts a height of $-40$ centimeters at week 20. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The prediction is reliable, because r squared is close to 1 for these data
The plant will shrink to a position below the ground by week 20
The data from weeks 1 through 6 must be wrong, since the model gives a negative value
The prediction is outside the data and unreliable; a height cannot be negative
questions.answer: The prediction is outside the data and unreliable; a height cannot be negative
questions.solution: A model is only trustworthy near the data it was fit to. Week 20 is far outside weeks 1 through 6 (extrapolation), and a negative height is impossible, so the prediction is meaningless. A high r squared describes the fit within the data, not outside it.

solve.answer: The prediction is outside the data and unreliable; a height cannot be negative
solve.work: Week 20 is far outside weeks 1 to 6 (extrapolation); a negative height is impossible, so the prediction is unreliable despite the high r^2.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for the weekly revenue $R$, in hundreds of dollars, at a ticket price of $x$ dollars is $R = -2x^2 + 16x + 3$. At what price $x$ does the model predict the greatest revenue?
questions.solution: The graph of $R$ is a downward-opening parabola, so its highest point is at the vertex, $x = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{16}{2(-2)} = 4$ dollars.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for the height $h$, in feet, of a ball $t$ seconds after it is hit is $h = -16t^2 + 64t$. At what time $t > 0$ does the model predict that the ball is back on the ground?
questions.solution: Set $h = 0$: $-16t(t - 4) = 0$, so $t = 0$ or $t = 4$. The ball is back on the ground at $t = 4$ seconds.

questions.stem: An exponential regression model for the value $V$, in dollars, of a car $t$ years after it was bought is $V = 20000(0.8)^t$. What value does the model predict at $t = 2$?
An exponential regression model for the number of followers $N$ of a page $t$ weeks after it starts is $N = 1000(3)^t$. After how many weeks does the model predict 27000 followers?
The number of students who know a rumor starts at 8 and, according to an exponential regression model, triples every hour. Which equation gives the number $y$ who know the rumor after $x$ hours?
questions.solution: An exponential model has the form $y = a \cdot b^x$, where $a$ is the starting value 8 and $b$ is the multiplier per hour, 3. So $y = 8(3)^x$.

solve.work: Start 8, factor 3 per hour: y=8(3)^x.

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 4 + 3\log_2(x)$. How does the predicted value of $y$ change each time $x$ doubles?
choices: It increases by 3
It doubles
It increases by 6
It increases by 4
questions.answer: It increases by 3
questions.solution: Doubling $x$ adds 1 to $\log_2(x)$, so $y$ changes by $3 \times 1 = 3$. The change is the same every time $x$ doubles, whatever $x$ is.

solve.answer: It increases by 3
solve.work: log2(2x)=log2(x)+1, so y increases by 3.

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model $y = 12 + 5\ln(x)$ was fit to data with $x$ between 2 and 20. What does the model say about $x = 0$?
choices: It predicts $y = 12$, because the logarithm term vanishes
It predicts $y = 0$, because the log of zero is zero
It makes no prediction, because $\ln(0)$ is undefined
It predicts $y = 17$, because $\ln(0)$ equals 1
questions.answer: It makes no prediction, because $\ln(0)$ is undefined
questions.solution: The natural logarithm is defined only for positive numbers, so $\ln(0)$ does not exist and the model gives no value at $x = 0$.

solve.answer: It makes no prediction, because $\ln(0)$ is undefined
solve.work: ln(0) undefined (and 0 is outside the data), so no prediction.

questions.stem: A regression line is $\hat{y} = 3x + 2$. A data point is $(4, 17)$. What is the residual, using residual = actual value minus predicted value?
questions.solution: The predicted value at $x = 4$ is $3(4) + 2 = 14$. The actual value is 17, so the residual is $17 - 14 = 3$.

solve.work: Predicted 3*4+2=14; residual 17-14=3.

questions.stem: At the same data point, Model A has a residual of $-2$ and Model B has a residual of $+5$. Which model is closer to the actual value there?
choices: Model A, because the size of its residual is smaller
Model B, because its residual is positive
Model B, because 5 is greater than $-2$
Neither, because residuals with different signs cannot be compared
questions.answer: Model A, because the size of its residual is smaller
questions.solution: How close a model comes is the size of the residual, ignoring its sign: $|-2| = 2$ is less than $|5| = 5$. So Model A is closer.

solve.answer: Model A, because the size of its residual is smaller
solve.work: |-2| < |5|, so Model A is closer.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A residual plot for a regression model shows residuals close to zero for small values of $x$ and residuals far from zero, above and below, for large values of $x$. What does this suggest?
choices: The model fits the data better for large $x$ than for small $x$
The model is badly wrong for small $x$, so it should be rejected
The residuals must add up to a large number, so the model is biased
The spread of the errors is not constant, so predictions are less reliable for large $x$
questions.answer: The spread of the errors is not constant, so predictions are less reliable for large $x$
questions.solution: Residuals that fan out as $x$ grows mean the errors are larger when $x$ is large, so the model's predictions there are less reliable.

solve.answer: The spread of the errors is not constant, so predictions are less reliable for large $x$
solve.work: Fan shape: non-constant spread, less reliable for large x.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: The residuals of a model at five data points are $2$, $-3$, $1$, $-1$ and $1$. What is the sum of the squares of the residuals?
questions.solution: Square each residual and add: $4 + 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 16$. A model with a smaller sum of squared residuals fits the same data better.

questions.stem: A linear model with an upward-sloping line has $r^2 = 0.64$. What is $r$?
questions.solution: $r$ is the square root of $r^2$, so $r = \pm 0.8$. The line slopes upward, so $r$ is positive: $r = 0.8$.

solve.work: r=+sqrt(0.64)=0.8 (positive slope).

questions.stem: Four linear models are fit to four different data sets, with $r$ values of $0.7$, $-0.9$, $0.2$ and $-0.5$. Which model shows the strongest linear relationship?
questions.solution: Strength depends on how far $r$ is from 0, not on its sign. The value $-0.9$ is closest to $-1$, so it shows the strongest relationship.

solve.work: Largest |r| is 0.9 for r=-0.9.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A table shows $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$ and $y = 2, 6, 18, 54$. An exponential model fits these values exactly. What does the model predict for $y$ at $x = 4$?
questions.solution: Each y-value is 3 times the one before, so the model multiplies by 3 for each step of $x$. At $x = 4$: $54 \times 3 = 162$.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A table shows $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ and $y = 1, 3, 7, 13, 21$. The differences between consecutive y-values are $2, 4, 6, 8$. Which regression model type fits these values exactly?
choices: Linear, because every difference is positive, so y rises at every step
Exponential, because y is always increasing and gets larger at each step
Logarithmic, because y is always increasing from each step to the next
Quadratic, because the differences themselves increase by a constant 2
questions.answer: Quadratic, because the differences themselves increase by a constant 2
questions.solution: A linear model has constant differences, and an exponential model has constant ratios. Here the second differences (the changes in the differences) are constant at 2, which is the signature of a quadratic. In fact $y = x^2 + x + 1$ fits every row.

solve.answer: Quadratic, because the differences themselves increase by a constant 2
solve.work: Second differences constant 2: quadratic.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A quadratic model fits the table $x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $y = 2, 5, 10, 17, 26$ exactly. What does it predict for $y$ at $x = 6$?
questions.solution: Each y-value is one more than $x^2$: $1 + 1 = 2$, $4 + 1 = 5$, $9 + 1 = 10$, and so on. So $y = x^2 + 1$, and at $x = 6$ it is $36 + 1 = 37$. (The differences 3, 5, 7, 9 grow by 2, so the next is 11 and $26 + 11 = 37$.)

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: A population of 2000 grows by 15 percent each year, according to an exponential model. Which equation gives the population $y$ after $x$ years?
questions.solution: Growing by 15 percent each year multiplies the population by $1 + 0.15 = 1.15$ each year, so $y = 2000(1.15)^x$.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: In a data set, one point lies far from all the others and pulls the fitted curve strongly toward it. What is the best next step?
choices: Delete the point without saying so, since it makes the fit worse
Investigate the point, and report the model with and without it
Keep the point and ignore its effect, since all data must be used
Replace the point with the mean of the other $y$-values
questions.answer: Investigate the point, and report the model with and without it
questions.solution: An unusual point may be a recording error or a real, important case. A careful analyst finds out which, and shows how much the conclusion depends on the point.

solve.answer: Investigate the point, and report the model with and without it
solve.work: Investigate an influential point and report with and without it.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: A quadratic regression model was fit to data with $x$ from 2 to 10. For which value of $x$ is its prediction the most trustworthy?
questions.solution: A prediction is most trustworthy inside the range of the data, and $x = 6$ is the only value in the range from 2 to 10. The others are extrapolations, and $x = 40$ is the farthest.

solve.work: x=6 lies within 2 to 10 (interpolation).

questions.skill: Use a model with two or more predictors
questions.stem: A model predicts the monthly rent $R$, in dollars, of an apartment: $R = 300 + 0.8A - 20D$, where $A$ is the area in square feet and $D$ is the distance in miles from the city center. What rent does it predict for an apartment with $A = 900$ and $D = 5$?

questions.skill: Use a model with two or more predictors
questions.stem: A model is $\hat{y} = 10 + 3x_1 - 4x_2$. How does the predicted value change if $x_1$ increases by 2 and $x_2$ increases by 1?
choices: It increases by 2
It increases by 6
It decreases by 4
It increases by 5
questions.answer: It increases by 2
questions.solution: The change is $3(2) - 4(1) = 6 - 4 = 2$, so the prediction increases by 2. The constant 10 does not affect changes.

solve.answer: It increases by 2
solve.work: 3*2-4*1=2, increases by 2.

questions.stem: A student wants to check whether data follow an exponential pattern $y = a \cdot b^x$. Which new plot would look like a straight line if the pattern is exponential?
choices: $y$ against $\ln(x)$
$y$ against $x^2$
$\ln(y)$ against $x$
$y$ against $\sqrt{x}$
questions.answer: $\ln(y)$ against $x$
questions.solution: Taking logarithms of $y = a \cdot b^x$ gives $\ln(y) = \ln(a) + x\ln(b)$, which is a straight line when $\ln(y)$ is plotted against $x$.

solve.answer: $\ln(y)$ against $x$
solve.work: ln(y)=ln(a)+x ln(b), linear in x: plot ln(y) against x.

questions.stem: For some data, a straight line fit to $\log_{10}(y)$ against $x$ is $\log_{10}(y) = 1 + 2x$. According to the model, what is $y$ when $x = 1$?
A regression model predicts $y = 2x^2$. The actual values at $x = 1, 2, 3$ are 3, 7 and 20. What is the sum of the three residuals (actual minus predicted)?
questions.solution: The predictions are 2, 8 and 18. The residuals are $3 - 2 = 1$, $7 - 8 = -1$ and $20 - 18 = 2$. Their sum is $1 - 1 + 2 = 2$.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A quadratic regression model has $r^2 = 0.95$, but its residual plot shows a clear wave-shaped pattern. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The model is certainly appropriate, because its r squared is so high
A high r squared does not by itself show the model is right; try another type
The residual plot must be wrong, because r squared is so high
The model is useless, because r squared is always misleading and never helpful
questions.answer: A high r squared does not by itself show the model is right; try another type
questions.solution: A high r squared says the model explains a lot of the variation, but a clear pattern in the residuals shows a systematic way in which the model misses the data. Both pieces of evidence should be used, so a different model type should be tried. Neither one overrules the other, and r squared is not worthless.

solve.answer: A high r squared does not by itself show the model is right; try another type
solve.work: A systematic residual pattern shows the model misses structure even with a high r^2; r^2 alone does not confirm the model, so try another type.

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 6 + 4 \cdot \text{ln}(x)$. What does it predict at $x = e^3$? (Use $\text{ln}(e^3) = 3$.)
questions.solution: Substitute $x = e^3$: $y = 6 + 4 \cdot \text{ln}(e^3) = 6 + 4 \cdot 3 = 18$.

questions.stem: An exponential model $y = a \cdot b^x$, with $b > 0$, passes through the points $(0, 5)$ and $(2, 45)$. What does the model predict at $x = 3$?

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: To fit an exponential model, a student fits a line to $\text{ln}(y)$ against x and gets $\text{ln}(y) = 1.2 + 0.5x$. Which statement correctly describes the exponential model?
choices: Each time x increases by 1, y is multiplied by 1.5, since 1 + 0.5 = 1.5
Each time x increases by 1, y increases by 0.5, the slope of the line
Each time x increases by 1, y is multiplied by $e^{0.5}$ (about 1.65)
Each time x increases by 1, y is multiplied by 0.5, the slope of the line
questions.answer: Each time x increases by 1, y is multiplied by $e^{0.5}$ (about 1.65)
questions.solution: Raising e to both sides gives $y = e^{1.2} \cdot (e^{0.5})^x$. So y is multiplied by $e^{0.5}$, which is about 1.65, each time x increases by 1. The slope 0.5 is added to ln y, which multiplies y; it is not added to y or used as the multiplier itself.

solve.answer: Each time x increases by 1, y is multiplied by $e^{0.5}$ (about 1.65)
solve.work: ln y = 1.2 + 0.5x gives y = e^1.2 * (e^0.5)^x, so y is multiplied by e^0.5 (about 1.6487, about 1.65) per unit of x.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A table shows $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ and $y = 80, 40, 20, 10, 5$. Which equation fits all five values exactly?
questions.solution: Each y is half the one before, so y is multiplied by 0.5 for each step, starting at 80 when $x = 0$: $y = 80(0.5)^x$. Check: $x = 2$ gives $80 \times 0.25 = 20$. The other equations start or change wrongly (for example, $y = 80 - 40x$ gives 0 at $x = 2$).

solve.work: Starts at 80 and halves each step: y = 80(0.5)^x gives 80, 40, 20, 10, 5. 80 - 40x gives 0 at x = 2; 40(0.5)^x starts at 40; 80(2)^x grows.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: A model fit to monthly data shows ice cream sales and sunburn cases rising and falling together, with $r^2 = 0.91$. A newspaper says that ice cream sales cause sunburns. What is the best response?
choices: The high r squared shows that eating ice cream causes sunburn
The two cannot be related at all, because neither one causes the other
A nonlinear model can prove cause, which a linear model cannot
The data show only an association; sunny weather may drive both
questions.answer: The data show only an association; sunny weather may drive both
questions.solution: A strong fit shows that two variables move together, not that one causes the other. A lurking variable, here hot sunny weather, can raise both. Evidence of cause needs a carefully designed experiment, not a higher r squared or a different type of curve.

solve.answer: The data show only an association; sunny weather may drive both
solve.work: A strong association does not show causation; a lurking variable (sunny, hot weather) likely drives both.

questions.stem: A linearized exponential model has $r = -0.9$. What percent of the variation in $\text{ln}(y)$ is NOT explained by the model?
questions.solution: The value of r squared is $(-0.9)^2 = 0.81$, so 81 percent of the variation is explained. The rest, $100 - 81 = 19$ percent, is not explained. (The sign of r does not matter for r squared.)

solve.work: r^2 = (-0.9)^2 = 0.81, so 81 percent is explained and 100 - 81 = 19 percent is not.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A table shows $x = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16$ and $y = 3, 5, 7, 9, 11$. Which type of regression model fits these values exactly?
choices: Linear: y increases by the same amount each time x increases by 1
Logarithmic: y increases by the same amount each time x doubles
Exponential: y is multiplied by the same factor each time x doubles
Quadratic: the increases in y get larger as x gets larger
questions.answer: Logarithmic: y increases by the same amount each time x doubles
questions.solution: Each time x doubles (1 to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 16), y goes up by the same 2. Equal increases in y for equal factors in x is the signature of a logarithmic model, $y = 3 + 2 \cdot \text{log}_2(x)$. The increases in y are constant, not growing, so it is not quadratic, and y is not multiplied by a constant factor.

solve.answer: Logarithmic: y increases by the same amount each time x doubles
solve.work: Each time x doubles (1, 2, 4, 8, 16), y rises by 2: y = 3 + 2 log2(x), a logarithmic model. Not linear (x steps differ), not quadratic, not exponential.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model is $y = -x^2 + 10x$. The model predicts $y = 21$ at two values of x. What is the larger of the two values?
questions.solution: Set $-x^2 + 10x = 21$, so $x^2 - 10x + 21 = 0$. This factors as $(x - 3)(x - 7) = 0$, so $x = 3$ or $x = 7$. The larger is 7. (The two values are symmetric about the vertex at $x = 5$.)

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model is $y = x^2 - 10x + 30$. The model predicts $y = 7$ at two values of $x$. What is the sum of these two values of $x$?
questions.solution: Setting $y = 7$ gives $x^2 - 10x + 23 = 0$, which has two solutions whose sum is $-\frac{b}{a} = 10$. (Equivalently, the two values are symmetric about the vertex at $x = 5$.)

solve.work: x^2-10x+23=0 (discriminant 8>0, two real roots); sum of roots = 10.

questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for the number of visitors $N$ at a museum, $t$ hours after it opens, is $N = -2t^2 + 16t + 20$. Which statement about the greatest number of visitors the model predicts is correct?
choices: 20 visitors, at 4 hours after opening
52 visitors, at 4 hours after opening
52 visitors, at 8 hours after opening
76 visitors, at 4 hours after opening
questions.answer: 52 visitors, at 4 hours after opening
questions.solution: The vertex is at $t = -\frac{16}{2(-2)} = 4$. There, $N = -2(16) + 16(4) + 20 = -32 + 64 + 20 = 52$. The value 20 is the prediction at opening ($t = 0$), and 76 comes from dropping the square.

solve.answer: 52 visitors, at 4 hours after opening

questions.stem: An exponential model $y = a \cdot b^x$, with $b > 0$, passes through the points $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 54)$. What does the model predict at $x = 4$?
questions.solution: Going from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$ multiplies $y$ by $\frac{54}{6} = 9$, which is $b^2$, so $b = 3$. Then $y$ at $x = 4$ is $54 \times 3 = 162$.

questions.stem: A radioactive sample is modeled by $y = 80(0.5)^{t/3}$, where $y$ is the mass in grams and $t$ is the time in days. What mass does the model predict at $t = 9$ days?
questions.solution: At $t = 9$, the exponent is $\frac{9}{3} = 3$, so $y = 80(0.5)^3 = 80 \times 0.125 = 10$ grams. (The mass halves every 3 days.)

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 1 + 2\log_{10}(x)$. For what value of $x$ does the model predict $y = 7$?

questions.skill: Use and interpret a fitted logarithmic model
questions.stem: A logarithmic regression model is $y = 4 + 2\ln(x)$. How much larger is the predicted value at $x = 3e$ than at $x = 3$? (Here $e$ is the constant with $\ln(e) = 1$.)
questions.solution: The difference is $2\ln(3e) - 2\ln(3) = 2(\ln(3e) - \ln(3)) = 2\ln\left(\frac{3e}{3}\right) = 2\ln(e) = 2$.

questions.stem: A regression model is $\hat{y} = 0.5x^2$. The actual values at $x = 2, 4$ and $6$ are 3, 5 and 22. What is the largest absolute value among the three residuals?
questions.solution: The predictions are $0.5(4) = 2$, $0.5(16) = 8$ and $0.5(36) = 18$. The residuals (actual $-$ predicted) are $1$, $-3$ and $4$. The largest absolute value is 4.

solve.work: Predictions 2, 8, 18. Residuals 1, -3, 4. Largest absolute value 4.

questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $\hat{y} = 120(0.9)^x$. At $x = 2$ the actual value is 100. What is the residual, using residual = actual value minus predicted value?
questions.solution: The predicted value is $120(0.9)^2 = 120 \times 0.81 = 97.2$. The residual is $100 - 97.2 = 2.8$.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: Model 1 has $r^2 = 0.88$ and a residual plot with a random scatter. Model 2, for the same data, has $r^2 = 0.93$ and a residual plot with a strong curved pattern. Which conclusion is best?
choices: Model 2 is preferable, because its larger $r^2$ shows it explains more of the variation
Model 1 is preferable, because the curved pattern shows that Model 2 is the wrong type of model
Model 1 is preferable, because a smaller $r^2$ always means a simpler model
The two models are equally good, because both have an $r^2$ above 0.85
questions.answer: Model 1 is preferable, because the curved pattern shows that Model 2 is the wrong type of model
questions.solution: A curved pattern in the residuals shows that the model type does not match the data, even when $r^2$ is high. The random scatter for Model 1 shows its type suits the data, so it is the better choice.

solve.answer: Model 1 is preferable, because the curved pattern shows that Model 2 is the wrong type of model
solve.work: Curved residual pattern shows Model 2 is the wrong form despite higher r^2; prefer Model 1.

questions.skill: Judge fit from residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A least-squares line is fit to 5 data points. Four of the residuals are $1.5$, $-2$, $0.5$ and $3$. What is the fifth residual?
questions.solution: The residuals of a least-squares line (with an intercept) always add up to 0. The four known residuals add to $1.5 - 2 + 0.5 + 3 = 3$, so the fifth residual is $-3$.

solve.work: Least-squares line residuals sum to 0: 1.5-2+0.5+3=3, fifth = -3.

questions.stem: For a data set, $r = 0$ for the best straight line. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: There is no linear relationship, but there could still be a strong curved relationship
There is no relationship of any kind between $x$ and $y$, curved or straight
The data must lie on a perfect curve that $r$ cannot detect
The line must be horizontal and all the data must lie exactly on it
questions.answer: There is no linear relationship, but there could still be a strong curved relationship
questions.solution: The correlation $r$ measures only linear association. Data that follow a clear parabola, for example, can have $r$ near 0.

solve.answer: There is no linear relationship, but there could still be a strong curved relationship
solve.work: r=0 means no linear relationship; a curved one may still exist.

questions.stem: The total variation in $y$ (the sum of the squared differences from the mean of $y$) is 200. A regression model has $r^2 = 0.85$. How much of that variation is left unexplained?
questions.solution: The model explains 85 percent of the variation, so 15 percent is unexplained: $0.15 \times 200 = 30$.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: The population of a species in a new habitat grows fast at first, and then levels off as food runs short. An exponential regression model fits the first few years well. What is the main danger in using it for later years?
choices: It cannot predict any value at all after the first few years of data
It keeps growing without bound, so it will over-predict once the population is limited
It makes the population shrink as soon as the food runs short
It predicts a population that is smaller than the true one in later years
questions.answer: It keeps growing without bound, so it will over-predict once the population is limited
questions.solution: An exponential model has no ceiling. Real populations are limited by resources, so far beyond the data the model grows past what is possible and over-predicts.

solve.answer: It keeps growing without bound, so it will over-predict once the population is limited
solve.work: Exponential grows without bound; over-predicts once population levels off.

questions.skill: Choose a regression model type from a pattern
questions.stem: A scatterplot shows $y$ rising, then falling, then rising again as $x$ increases. What is the lowest-degree polynomial regression model that could follow this pattern?
choices: Linear
Quadratic
Quartic
Cubic
questions.answer: Cubic
questions.solution: A quadratic has one turning point. A pattern that rises, falls and rises again has two turning points, and a cubic is the lowest-degree polynomial that can have two.

solve.answer: Cubic
solve.work: Rise-fall-rise needs two turning points: cubic.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: An exponential regression model is $y = 80(1.5)^x$. What is the smallest whole number $x$ for which the model predicts $y$ greater than 400?
questions.solution: Try whole numbers: at $x = 3$, $y = 80(3.375) = 270$, which is less than 400. At $x = 4$, $y = 80(5.0625) = 405$, which is greater than 400. So the smallest whole $x$ is 4.

questions.skill: Interpret the growth or decay factor of an exponential model
questions.stem: Two exponential regression models are $y = 20(1.6)^x$ and $z = 100(1.2)^x$. Which statement is correct for large $x$?
choices: $z$ stays larger than $y$, because its starting value is larger
$z$ eventually exceeds $y$, because its starting value is larger
$y$ eventually exceeds $z$, because its growth factor is larger
$y$ and $z$ stay the same distance apart for all $x$
questions.answer: $y$ eventually exceeds $z$, because its growth factor is larger
questions.solution: The model with the larger growth factor eventually wins, whatever the starting values. Here $\frac{y}{z} = \frac{20}{100}\left(\frac{1.6}{1.2}\right)^x$ grows without bound, and passes 1 at about $x = 5.6$.

solve.answer: $y$ eventually exceeds $z$, because its growth factor is larger
solve.work: Larger growth factor eventually dominates: y exceeds z.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: An exponential model for the number of users of an app, in thousands, is $y = 2(1.5)^x$, where $x$ is the number of months since launch. The servers can handle 20 thousand users. What is the first whole month $x$ in which the model predicts more users than the servers can handle?
questions.solution: Try whole months: at $x = 5$, $y = 2(7.59) = 15.2$, below 20. At $x = 6$, $y = 2(11.39) = 22.8$, above 20. So the first month is $x = 6$.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: Two models are fit to the same data with $x$ up to 12. Both have $r^2 = 0.95$, but they give very different predictions at $x = 30$. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The model with the simpler equation must be right at $x = 30$, since simple models extrapolate best
A good fit within the data does not tell which model extrapolates correctly, so the prediction at $x = 30$ is uncertain
The average of the two predictions must be correct, since the models fit equally well
The predictions must be equal, because both $r^2$ values are the same
questions.answer: A good fit within the data does not tell which model extrapolates correctly, so the prediction at $x = 30$ is uncertain
questions.solution: Both models describe the data equally well, but they continue in different ways. The data cannot show which continuation is right, so a prediction far outside the data is uncertain.

solve.answer: A good fit within the data does not tell which model extrapolates correctly, so the prediction at $x = 30$ is uncertain
solve.work: Equal fit within data says nothing about extrapolation; prediction at 30 uncertain.

questions.skill: Draw evidence-based conclusions from a model
questions.stem: In a hospital, patients who got more doses of a medicine had worse outcomes, with $r = -0.7$. A manager concludes that the medicine harms patients. What is the best response?
choices: The conclusion is correct, because a negative $r$ shows that the doses do harm
The conclusion is correct, because a value of $-0.7$ is strong enough to show cause
Sicker patients may get more doses, so something other than the dose may explain the pattern
The data prove that the medicine helps, because $r$ is not exactly $-1$
questions.answer: Sicker patients may get more doses, so something other than the dose may explain the pattern
questions.solution: This is observational data. Patients who are sicker may be given more doses and also have worse outcomes, so the dose may not be the cause. Correlation alone does not show harm.

solve.answer: Sicker patients may get more doses, so something other than the dose may explain the pattern
solve.work: Confounding: sicker patients may get more doses.

questions.skill: Use a model with two or more predictors
questions.stem: A model is $\hat{y} = 5 + 2x_1 + 3x_2$. When $x_1 = 4$, what value of $x_2$ gives a predicted value of 28?

questions.skill: Use a model with two or more predictors
questions.stem: A model predicts the price $P$ of a house, in thousands of dollars: $P = 20 + 0.1a + 12b$, where $a$ is the area in square feet and $b$ is the number of bathrooms. A house with $a = 1500$ and $b = 2$ sold for 205 thousand dollars. What is the residual, using residual = actual value minus predicted value?
questions.solution: The predicted price is $20 + 0.1(1500) + 12(2) = 20 + 150 + 24 = 194$ thousand dollars. The residual is $205 - 194 = 11$ thousand dollars.

questions.stem: A straight line fit to $\log_{10}(y)$ against $x$ passes through $(0, 2)$, $(1, 3)$ and $(2, 4)$. According to the model, what is $y$ when $x = 3$?
questions.solution: The line is $\log_{10}(y) = 2 + x$. At $x = 3$, $\log_{10}(y) = 5$, so $y = 10^5 = 100000$. (So $y = 100 \cdot 10^x$: it is multiplied by 10 for each step of $x$.)

solve.work: log y = 2 + x; at x=3, log y=5, y=100000.

questions.stem: A line fit to $\ln(y)$ against $x$ has slope $-0.2$. Which statement about $y$ is correct?
choices: $y$ decreases by exactly 0.2 each time $x$ increases by 1, so it falls in a straight line
$y$ decays exponentially: each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ is multiplied by $e^{-0.2}$, about 0.82
$y$ decreases by exactly 20 percent each time $x$ increases by 1, because the slope is $-0.2$
$y$ grows exponentially, because the plot of $\ln(y)$ against $x$ is a straight line
questions.answer: $y$ decays exponentially: each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ is multiplied by $e^{-0.2}$, about 0.82
questions.solution: If $\ln(y) = c - 0.2x$, then $y = e^c \cdot e^{-0.2x} = e^c(e^{-0.2})^x$. Each step of 1 in $x$ multiplies $y$ by $e^{-0.2} \approx 0.82$, a decrease of about 18 percent, not exactly 20.

solve.answer: $y$ decays exponentially: each time $x$ increases by 1, $y$ is multiplied by $e^{-0.2}$, about 0.82
solve.work: ln y = c - 0.2x -> y multiplied by e^{-0.2} ~ 0.82 each unit.

questions.stem: A class is planning an investigation. Here are three questions. (1) How many pets do the students in our class have? (2) How many pets does Maria have? (3) What is a typical number of pets for students at our school? A statistical question is one that expects the answers to vary and can be answered by collecting data. How many of the three questions are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Question (1) expects different answers from different students, and so does question (3), so both are statistical questions. Question (2) asks about one person and has a single answer. So 2 of the questions are statistical.

solve.work: (1) Pets of students in our class: answers vary by student, collect data -> statistical. (2) Maria's pets: one fixed answer -> not statistical. (3) Typical number of pets at school: variability expected -> statistical. Count = 2.

questions.stem: A student wants to find out how much time students at her school spend on homework. Which survey question is the clearest and the least biased?
choices: Do you do a lot of homework, or only a little, compared with other students at your school?
On a typical school night, about how many minutes do you spend on homework outside of class?
Don't you agree that teachers give students far too much homework every single night?
How much time do you spend on homework, reading and studying each week or each day?
questions.answer: On a typical school night, about how many minutes do you spend on homework outside of class?
questions.solution: A good question names the quantity (minutes of homework), the time period (a typical school night) and does not push the answer. "A lot" means different things to different people, the question that starts "Don't you agree" leads the student toward yes, and the last question mixes several activities and two different time periods.

solve.answer: On a typical school night, about how many minutes do you spend on homework outside of class?
solve.work: D names a clear unit (minutes), a clear time frame (a typical school night) and is neutral. A is vague/comparative, B mixes activities and time frames, C is leading.

questions.stem: A school has 1200 students. The student council wants to know the favorite lunch of all students. Which sample is most likely to represent all of the students?
choices: The first 100 students who walk into the school building on Monday morning
100 students taken from the line at the cafeteria window that sells pizza
The 100 students who choose to answer an online poll that the council posts
100 students picked by a random number generator from the list of all students
questions.answer: 100 students picked by a random number generator from the list of all students
questions.solution: A simple random sample gives every student the same chance to be chosen, so it is likely to represent the school. Early arrivals, a line for one food and volunteers who answer a poll are all groups that may differ from the rest of the students.

solve.answer: 100 students picked by a random number generator from the list of all students
solve.work: A simple random sample from the full list gives every student an equal chance. The others are convenience or voluntary-response samples.

questions.stem: A school has 600 students: 360 girls and 240 boys. A stratified random sample of 50 students has the same percent of boys as the school. How many boys should be in the sample?
questions.solution: Boys are $\frac{240}{600}=40\%$ of the school. The sample should also be 40% boys: $0.40\times 50=20$ boys.

questions.stem: A probability model for a spinner gives red 0.2, blue 0.5 and green 0.1. The only other color on the spinner is yellow. What probability must the model give to yellow?
questions.solution: The probabilities of all the outcomes in a model must add to 1. The three given add to $0.2+0.5+0.1=0.8$, so yellow must have $1-0.8=0.2$.

solve.work: Probabilities sum to 1: 1 - (0.2 + 0.5 + 0.1) = 0.2.

questions.stem: Mia surveyed 40 students in her school's choir, and 80% said they like jazz. Which statement is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Among the 40 choir students surveyed, 80% like jazz; this may not hold for all students
80% of all students at the school like jazz, since the choir is a part of the whole school
80% of all students in the whole country like jazz, as the survey shows
Jazz is the favorite kind of music of 80% of the students in the school choir
questions.answer: Among the 40 choir students surveyed, 80% like jazz; this may not hold for all students
questions.solution: The choir students are not a random sample of the school, so the 80% describes only the students surveyed. It cannot be stated for the whole school or the country, and "like jazz" does not mean jazz is their favorite.

solve.answer: Among the 40 choir students surveyed, 80% like jazz; this may not hold for all students
solve.work: Sample is choir students only, so the result describes those 40 and may not generalize. 'Like jazz' is not 'favorite', so B misstates it.

questions.stem: A study of 30 towns finds that towns with higher ice cream sales also have more cases of sunburn. A newspaper writes that ice cream causes sunburn. What is the best critique?
choices: Sunburn must be causing people to buy more ice cream, so the cause runs the other way
The association is not real, because ice cream is not a cause of sunburn in any way
Hot weather could raise both ice cream sales and sunburns, so cause is not shown
Cause and effect is proven, because the study included as many as 30 different towns
questions.answer: Hot weather could raise both ice cream sales and sunburns, so cause is not shown
questions.solution: Two variables that rise together may both be driven by a third variable, here the weather. An association alone does not show that one causes the other. The association in the data is real, and a larger number of towns does not turn an observation into proof of cause.

solve.answer: Hot weather could raise both ice cream sales and sunburns, so cause is not shown
solve.work: Association in an observational study; a lurking variable (hot weather) can drive both, so causation is not shown.

questions.stem: An ad says, "9 out of 10 users love our app." The company asked 10 people it chose itself. What is the main concern?
choices: Nine out of 10 is too high a percent to ever be possible for a real app
The ad should have used a pie chart instead of a sentence to show the result
Only 10 people, picked by the company, were asked, so they may not represent users
Ten people is always enough, as long as most of them agree with each other
questions.answer: Only 10 people, picked by the company, were asked, so they may not represent users
questions.solution: A sample of 10 is very small, and people picked by the company are probably not typical of all users, so the result may be far from the truth. A high percent is possible, the type of display is not the issue, and agreement among a few people does not make a sample large enough.
