solve.answer: Only 10 people, picked by the company, were asked, so they may not represent users
solve.work: Tiny, self-selected sample chosen by the company: likely biased, not representative of users.

questions.stem: The percent of voters who support a proposal rose from 38% to 45%. By how many percentage points did it rise?
questions.solution: A change between two percents is reported in percentage points: $45-38=7$ percentage points.

solve.work: 45% - 38% = 7 percentage points.

questions.stem: A student surveyed 120 workers about their commute and found a median of 25 minutes. Which sentence communicates the result best?
choices: The median commute time of the 120 workers surveyed was 25 minutes.
The median was 25 for the workers who answered the survey.
The commute time is 25 minutes for the workers in the whole city.
The surveyed workers have commutes that are long and about the same.
questions.answer: The median commute time of the 120 workers surveyed was 25 minutes.
questions.solution: A clear report names the statistic (median), the quantity and its unit (commute time, minutes) and the group (the 120 workers surveyed). The other sentences leave out the unit or the group, claim a single value for everyone, or give no number at all.

solve.answer: The median commute time of the 120 workers surveyed was 25 minutes.
solve.work: C states the statistic (median), the variable with units (commute time, minutes) and the group it describes (the 120 surveyed). A overgeneralizes, B lacks units/context, D is unsupported.

questions.stem: Which of these is a statistical question, one that expects the answers to vary and can be answered by collecting data?
choices: How many minutes did it take Dev to get to school this morning on the bus that he rides?
What time does the first bell of the school day ring at our school on a normal morning?
How many minutes does it take the students in our grade to get to school each morning?
How many students are in Ms. Lee's homeroom on the very first day of the school year?
questions.answer: How many minutes does it take the students in our grade to get to school each morning?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects different answers from different people, so data from many students are needed. The other three questions each have a single answer.

solve.answer: How many minutes does it take the students in our grade to get to school each morning?
solve.work: A is a fixed fact, B a single count, D one person once. Only the travel times of all students in the grade vary and are collected as data.

questions.stem: A student council wants to know how students feel about adding a second recess. Which survey question is the most neutral?
choices: Would you like a second recess added to the school day: yes, no, or not sure?
Wouldn't you agree that adding a second recess would obviously be great for every single student?
Don't you think that a useless extra recess would waste time that students need for their learning?
How much do you love the idea of getting a fun second recess added to the school day for everyone?
questions.answer: Would you like a second recess added to the school day: yes, no, or not sure?
questions.solution: The other questions push the student toward one answer with loaded words. The neutral question offers fair choices.

solve.answer: Would you like a second recess added to the school day: yes, no, or not sure?
solve.work: A offers yes/no/not sure with no loaded words; B, C, D use leading or loaded language.

questions.stem: To estimate how many people in a town own a car, a researcher stops people who are leaving a car dealership. Why might the sample give a biased estimate?
choices: The researcher can only count the people who are leaving the dealership, and not the people who are entering it
A sample of people from a town must include at least half of the people of the town to be unbiased
People at a car dealership are more likely to own or want a car than the people in the town as a whole
Car owners do not tend to visit dealerships, so the estimate of how many own a car will be too small
questions.answer: People at a car dealership are more likely to own or want a car than the people in the town as a whole
questions.solution: The people at a dealership are not like the whole town: they are more likely to be interested in cars. The sample was not random.

solve.answer: People at a car dealership are more likely to own or want a car than the people in the town as a whole
solve.work: People leaving a car dealership are more likely to own or want a car: selection bias, overestimate.

questions.stem: A club has 80 members: 40 sophomores, 24 juniors and 16 seniors. A stratified random sample of 20 members keeps the same percent of each class as the club. How many juniors are in the sample?
questions.solution: Juniors are 24 out of 80 members, which is 30%. 30% of 20 is 6.

solve.work: Juniors are 24/80 = 30% of the club; 30% of 20 = 6.

questions.stem: Why do researchers assign people to treatment groups at random in an experiment?
choices: So that the groups are likely to be alike in age, health and other ways before the treatment begins
So that every person in the study receives the treatment that is best for that particular person
So that the study will need fewer people than a study that does not use any random assignment
So that the people in the study cannot find out which of the two groups they have been placed in by the researcher
questions.answer: So that the groups are likely to be alike in age, health and other ways before the treatment begins
questions.solution: Random assignment tends to balance other factors between the groups, so a difference afterward can be credited to the treatment.

solve.answer: So that the groups are likely to be alike in age, health and other ways before the treatment begins
solve.work: Random assignment balances other variables between groups on average, so differences can be attributed to the treatment.

questions.stem: A principal picks a systematic sample from an alphabetical list of 480 students by choosing every 8th student on the list. How many students are in the sample?
questions.solution: Every 8th student out of 480 gives 480 divided by 8, which is 60 students.

questions.stem: A coin can land heads, tails or on its edge. Which is a valid probability model for one flip?
choices: Heads 0.49, tails 0.49, edge 0.02
Heads 0.50, tails 0.50, edge 0.02
Heads 0.48, tails 0.48, edge 0.02
Heads 0.60, tails -0.10, edge 0.50
questions.answer: Heads 0.49, tails 0.49, edge 0.02
questions.solution: A valid model has no negative probabilities and they add to 1. $0.49+0.49+0.02=1$. The first wrong model adds to 1.02, the second to 0.98, and the third has a negative probability.

solve.answer: Heads 0.49, tails 0.49, edge 0.02
solve.work: A: 0.49+0.49+0.02 = 1, all nonnegative. B sums to 1.02, C has a negative, D sums to 0.98.

questions.stem: A model says each seed has a 0.8 chance to sprout. How many of 150 seeds does the model expect to sprout?
questions.solution: The expected number is $0.8\times 150=120$.

questions.stem: A model says a coin is fair. A student flips the coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. What is the best statement?
choices: The model must be wrong, since a fair coin always gives exactly 5 heads when it is flipped 10 times
7 heads in 10 flips can easily happen by chance, so it is not strong evidence against the model
The model is proven wrong, since 7 heads is more than half of the 10 flips that the student made
The model is proven right, since 7 heads is close enough to the 5 heads that the model expects
questions.answer: 7 heads in 10 flips can easily happen by chance, so it is not strong evidence against the model
questions.solution: Small samples vary a lot. A fair coin gives 7 or more heads in 10 flips about 17% of the time, so this result does not rule the model out, and it does not prove the model either.

solve.answer: 7 heads in 10 flips can easily happen by chance, so it is not strong evidence against the model
solve.work: P(>=7 heads in 10 fair flips) = 176/1024 = 0.17, so 7 heads is quite possible by chance; not strong evidence against fairness.

questions.stem: In a computer simulation of a probability model, an event happened in 500 of 2000 trials. What is the estimated probability of the event?
questions.solution: The relative frequency is $\frac{500}{2000}=0.25$.

questions.stem: A survey finds that students who eat breakfast have higher grades on average than students who do not. Which is the best statement of the conclusion?
choices: Eating breakfast raises a student's grades, so every student should eat breakfast in order to improve their grades
Students who eat breakfast always have higher grades than students who skip it, whatever their other habits are
Grades have no connection at all to eating breakfast, since a survey like this one could not be done as an experiment
Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but the survey alone does not show that breakfast is the cause
questions.answer: Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but the survey alone does not show that breakfast is the cause
questions.solution: A survey shows an association. Other factors, such as sleep or family routines, could explain it, so cause is not shown.

solve.answer: Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but the survey alone does not show that breakfast is the cause
solve.work: Observational survey shows an association, not causation; C states the tendency without claiming cause.

questions.stem: A poll estimates that 38% of teens in a region play a sport, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. What is the highest percent that is plausible for all teens in the region?
questions.solution: The plausible values run from $38-3=35$ to $38+3=41$ percent, so the highest is 41.

questions.stem: A random sample of 50 students from a school of 800 has a mean of 6.5 hours of sleep per night. Which conclusion is best?
choices: The mean for all 800 students is probably close to 6.5 hours, though not necessarily exactly 6.5 hours
The mean for all 800 students is exactly 6.5 hours, because the sample of 50 students was chosen at random
Every student at the school sleeps close to 6.5 hours a night, so the mean is typical for each student there
The mean for all teenagers in the country is about 6.5 hours, since the sample was a random one
questions.answer: The mean for all 800 students is probably close to 6.5 hours, though not necessarily exactly 6.5 hours
questions.solution: A random sample estimates the population it came from (this school). The estimate is close to, but not exactly, the true mean, and it says nothing certain about other groups.

solve.answer: The mean for all 800 students is probably close to 6.5 hours, though not necessarily exactly 6.5 hours
solve.work: A random sample estimates the school mean; it is probably close to 6.5 but not exact, and applies to this school only.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly chooses 200 shoppers who are at one mall on a Saturday and asks about their spending. To which group can the results most reasonably be applied?
choices: People who shop at that mall on Saturdays, like the shoppers in the sample
All shoppers in the whole country on every day of the week, whichever store they go to
All people in the city, including the people who never shop at the mall on any day
All shoppers at every mall in the state, on weekdays as well as on weekends
questions.answer: People who shop at that mall on Saturdays, like the shoppers in the sample
questions.solution: Results apply to the population the sample was randomly drawn from: shoppers at that mall on Saturdays.

solve.answer: People who shop at that mall on Saturdays, like the shoppers in the sample
solve.work: The sample was of Saturday shoppers at one mall, so results generalize to that population.

questions.stem: A bar graph compares two companies' sales of 92 and 95 units. The vertical axis starts at 90, so the second bar looks 2.5 times as tall as the first. What is the problem with the graph?
choices: The bars should be drawn in the same order as the alphabet, with the company names in a line
Bar graphs can compare only percents of a total and never counts of units that were sold
The second bar should be drawn twice as wide as the first one, to show its higher sales
The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks much larger than it really is
questions.answer: The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks much larger than it really is
questions.solution: The bars start at 90, so their heights are 2 and 5 (a ratio of 2.5), but the sales are 92 and 95 (a ratio of about 1.03).

solve.answer: The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks much larger than it really is
solve.work: Bars from 90: heights 2 and 5, ratio 2.5, while 95/92 is only about 3% more. Truncated axis exaggerates the difference.

questions.stem: Sam flips a coin 4 times and gets 3 heads. He announces, "This coin is unfair; it lands on heads 75% of the time." What is the best critique?
choices: The percent is wrong, since 3 heads in 4 flips is 3 out of 4, which is 25% of the flips
Four flips are too few to tell, since 3 heads in 4 flips happens easily with a fair coin
A coin is shown to be fair if it gives any heads at all, so Sam should say the coin is fair
Flips of a coin cannot be used to study anything, since a coin has only two outcomes in total
questions.answer: Four flips are too few to tell, since 3 heads in 4 flips happens easily with a fair coin
questions.solution: A fair coin gives at least 3 heads in 4 flips 5 times in 16 (about 31%). A small sample cannot show the coin is unfair.

solve.answer: Four flips are too few to tell, since 3 heads in 4 flips happens easily with a fair coin
solve.work: P(3 or more heads in 4 fair flips) = 5/16; 3 heads in 4 is common, sample too small to conclude.

questions.stem: An ad says, "90% of customers are satisfied." The survey behind it found 27 satisfied customers out of 36 surveyed. What percent of the surveyed customers were actually satisfied?
questions.solution: $\frac{27}{36}=0.75$, so 75% were satisfied, not 90%.

questions.stem: A study paid for by the maker of a sugary drink reports that the drink is part of a healthy diet. Which is the best critique?
choices: The maker paid for the study, so the way it was designed and reported may favor the maker
A drink cannot be studied, since people drink different amounts of it from one day to the next
The study must be wrong, since any study that a company pays for is always false in what it reports
The study should have been paid for by a company that makes a different kind of drink
questions.answer: The maker paid for the study, so the way it was designed and reported may favor the maker
questions.solution: A source with something to gain may, even unintentionally, shape a study. We should look for independent studies. (It does not follow that the results are false.)

solve.answer: The maker paid for the study, so the way it was designed and reported may favor the maker
solve.work: Funding source creates a conflict of interest that may bias design or reporting; it does not make it automatically false.

questions.stem: In a survey of 250 students, 60 said they walk to school. What percent of the students surveyed walk to school?
Sixty students each named their favorite fruit: apple, banana or grape. Which is the best way to report the results?
choices: Give the mean favorite fruit, found by adding up all of the answers and dividing by the 60 students
Give the count or the percent of students who chose each fruit, in a table or a bar graph
Give the range of the fruits, found by subtracting the smallest fruit from the largest fruit
Give the median fruit, found by putting the 60 students in order by their height and taking the middle
questions.answer: Give the count or the percent of students who chose each fruit, in a table or a bar graph
questions.solution: Fruit names are categories, so we report how many chose each. Means, ranges and medians need numbers.

solve.answer: Give the count or the percent of students who chose each fruit, in a table or a bar graph
solve.work: Categorical data: report counts or percents per category in a table or bar graph.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives a reader the information needed to understand a survey result?
choices: Most students prefer a later start time, according to the survey of students that was done at one school in the spring
60% prefer a later start time, as was shown by the survey of students that the school carried out
Of 150 students at Maple Middle School who were randomly surveyed, 60% said they prefer a later start time
A survey showed that students prefer a later start time more than they prefer an earlier start time
questions.answer: Of 150 students at Maple Middle School who were randomly surveyed, 60% said they prefer a later start time
questions.solution: A clear report says who was surveyed, how many, how they were chosen and what the result was.

solve.answer: Of 150 students at Maple Middle School who were randomly surveyed, 60% said they prefer a later start time
solve.work: B gives the sample size, population, how chosen (random) and the result.

questions.stem: A student wants to know how students at her school feel about the new cafeteria menu. Which survey question does NOT push respondents toward a particular answer?
choices: Do you agree that the new menu is a big improvement over the old one?
Would you say the new menu is awful and should be changed right away?
How would you rate the new menu from 1 for poor to 5 for excellent?
Do you also love the new menu that most of the students already love?
questions.answer: How would you rate the new menu from 1 for poor to 5 for excellent?
questions.solution: A fair question uses neutral wording and lets every answer be given. The other questions suggest an answer by calling the menu an improvement, awful, or loved by most students. Only the rating question leaves the choice to the respondent.

solve.answer: How would you rate the new menu from 1 for poor to 5 for excellent?
solve.work: Options A, C and D are leading or loaded: they presuppose an improvement, appeal to popularity, or say 'awful'. The neutral rating scale from 1 to 5 is the unbiased question.

questions.stem: A survey asks students, "Do you think the cafeteria food is healthy and cheap?" What is the main problem with this question?
choices: It leads students toward answering yes by praising the food first
It asks about the past instead of asking about the cafeteria food now
It uses words that are much too difficult for most students to understand
It asks about two things at once, so one answer cannot fit both parts
questions.answer: It asks about two things at once, so one answer cannot fit both parts
questions.solution: A student who thinks the food is healthy but expensive cannot answer yes or no. A good question asks about one thing at a time, so "healthy" and "cheap" should be asked in two separate questions.

solve.answer: It asks about two things at once, so one answer cannot fit both parts
solve.work: Double-barreled question: food could be healthy but not cheap, so one yes/no cannot fit both.

questions.stem: A gardener tests whether a new fertilizer helps plants grow taller. She gives the new fertilizer to the plants in her sunny garden bed and no fertilizer to the plants in her shady bed, then compares the heights. What is the main flaw in this plan?
choices: Only one kind of fertilizer was tested, so there is nothing to compare
The amount of sunlight is mixed up with the fertilizer, so a difference could be due to either
The plants in the shady bed should have received more fertilizer than the plants in the sunny bed
The plants in the sunny bed should have received a second kind of fertilizer
questions.answer: The amount of sunlight is mixed up with the fertilizer, so a difference could be due to either
questions.solution: Sunny plants and shady plants differ in a second way besides the fertilizer, so the two effects cannot be separated. A better plan assigns the fertilizer to plants at random, from both beds, so that the sunlight is spread evenly over the two groups. One fertilizer compared with none is a fine comparison.

solve.answer: The amount of sunlight is mixed up with the fertilizer, so a difference could be due to either
solve.work: Treatment is confounded with sunlight (sunny bed gets fertilizer, shady bed none), so a height difference could be due to either.

questions.stem: A pollster wants a margin of error of about 0.05 (5 percentage points) for a random sample. Using the rough rule that the margin of error is about $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for a sample of size $n$, about how large a sample does she need?
A model says a die is fair, so each of the numbers 1 to 6 is equally likely. In 120 rolls, the die shows a 6 on 35 of the rolls. How many more 6s is this than the model expects?
questions.solution: The model expects a 6 on $\frac{1}{6}$ of the rolls: $120\div 6=20$ rolls. The die gave $35-20=15$ more 6s than the model expects.

questions.stem: A meteorologist models rain by saying each day has a 30% chance of rain, independent of the other days. Which is the main reason this model may be unrealistic?
choices: A chance of rain on a day cannot be as low as 30% in any real place
Rainy weather tends to last for several days, so the days are not independent
Rain either happens or it does not, so no probability can be given to it at all
Each day should have a 50% chance of rain, since there are two outcomes
questions.answer: Rainy weather tends to last for several days, so the days are not independent
questions.solution: Weather comes in spells: if it rained yesterday, rain today is more likely, so the days are not independent. A probability of 30% is allowed, probabilities are used for events that either happen or not, and two outcomes need not be equally likely.

solve.answer: Rainy weather tends to last for several days, so the days are not independent
solve.work: Weather is persistent from day to day, so the independence assumption is unrealistic. The other options are false reasoning.

questions.stem: In an experiment, 60 volunteers were randomly assigned to two groups of 30. One group took a new vitamin and the other took a placebo. The vitamin group had fewer colds over the winter, by more than chance would likely produce. The volunteers were not randomly chosen from all adults. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The vitamin reduces colds in all adults, since the groups were assigned at random
No cause-and-effect conclusion is possible at all, because the volunteers were not randomly chosen
The vitamin has no effect at all, because the volunteers were not randomly chosen
The vitamin probably reduced colds for volunteers like these, but this may not hold for all adults
questions.answer: The vitamin probably reduced colds for volunteers like these, but this may not hold for all adults
questions.solution: Random assignment to groups supports a cause-and-effect conclusion for the people in the study. Because the volunteers were not a random sample, the result may not apply to all adults. The lack of a random sample limits what the result is about, not whether the vitamin worked.

solve.answer: The vitamin probably reduced colds for volunteers like these, but this may not hold for all adults
solve.work: Random assignment supports a causal effect for these subjects; no random selection limits generalizing to all adults.

questions.stem: A random sample of 100 students finds that 62% prefer a later start time for school. Use a margin of error of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. What is the lowest percent of preference, in the population of all students, that is plausible?
questions.solution: The margin of error is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{100}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.10$, which is 10 percentage points. The lowest plausible value is $62-10=52$ percent.

solve.work: Margin = 1/sqrt(100) = 0.1 = 10 percentage points. Interval 62% +/- 10% = 52% to 72%. Lowest plausible: 52.

questions.stem: A news website asks readers to vote in an online poll about whether the city should build a new stadium. Of the 2000 readers who voted, 85% said yes, and the site reports, "Most residents support the stadium." What is the best critique?
choices: Readers chose whether to vote, so the voters may not represent all residents
2000 votes is too few for any poll to be useful, however the voters are chosen
85% is so high that the votes must have been counted wrongly by the website
The site should have reported the mean vote instead of the percent who said yes
questions.answer: Readers chose whether to vote, so the voters may not represent all residents
questions.solution: A poll that anyone may choose to answer attracts people with strong feelings, so its result may be far from the opinion of all residents, however many votes are cast. A large random sample of 2000 could be quite accurate, and a high percent is not a sign of miscounting.

solve.answer: Readers chose whether to vote, so the voters may not represent all residents
solve.work: Voluntary-response online poll of readers: self-selected, not representative of all residents.

questions.stem: A city says its new traffic program cut accidents by 30%, because there were 100 accidents last year, the worst year in a decade, and 70 accidents this year. What is the main concern?
choices: A drop of 30 accidents in one year is too small a change to be worth reporting to the public
Accidents should be reported as percents and never as counts of accidents in any report
Last year was unusually high, so the drop may be a return to normal, not due to the program
The program cannot have worked, because accidents did not fall all the way down to zero
questions.answer: Last year was unusually high, so the drop may be a return to normal, not due to the program
questions.solution: After an unusually bad year, the next year tends to be closer to normal even if nothing changes. Comparing with that one extreme year exaggerates the effect, so the claim needs more years of data or a comparison group. A drop to a lower number is not required to reach zero for a program to work.

solve.answer: Last year was unusually high, so the drop may be a return to normal, not due to the program
solve.work: Last year was the worst in a decade, so a drop is expected by regression to the mean; the drop may not be due to the program.

questions.stem: A report on typical pay at a small company lists the salaries, in thousands of dollars, of 6 workers: 38, 41, 44, 47, 52 and 250. The report uses the median because one very large salary pulls the mean up. What median, in thousands of dollars, should it report?
questions.solution: The salaries are already in order. With 6 values, the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: $\frac{44+47}{2}=45.5$ thousand dollars. The mean, $\frac{472}{6}\approx 78.7$, is pulled far up by the salary of 250.

questions.stem: A class lists five questions. (1) How tall are the players on our school's basketball teams? (2) How tall is Jordan, the center on one of those teams? (3) How much time do students in our grade spend on homework on a typical night? (4) Is the library open on Saturdays? (5) How do the test scores of students who sleep 8 hours compare with the scores of students who sleep 6 hours? A statistical question expects varying answers and can be answered by collecting data. How many of the five are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Questions 1, 3 and 5 expect answers that vary and need data from many people. Question 2 is about one person and question 4 has a single answer, so 3 are statistical.

solve.work: (1) heights vary: statistical. (2) one person: no. (3) homework time varies: yes. (4) single fact: no. (5) comparison of score distributions: yes. Total 3.

questions.stem: Half of a school's students, chosen at random, were asked, "Do you favor the new, modern, student-friendly uniform policy?" and 82% said yes. The other half were asked, "Do you favor forcing students to wear a uniform?" and only 31% said yes. What best explains the gap?
choices: The second half must have been a larger group, and a larger group always gives a lower percent of yes answers
The wording of each question pushes students toward a particular answer, so the results reflect the wording
Students answer differently on different days, so the same question never gives the same percent twice in a row
The two halves were chosen at random, which makes it likely that the two groups held completely opposite opinions
questions.answer: The wording of each question pushes students toward a particular answer, so the results reflect the wording
questions.solution: Both halves are random, so they should have similar opinions. A gap this large comes from the loaded wording of the two questions.

solve.answer: The wording of each question pushes students toward a particular answer, so the results reflect the wording
solve.work: Random halves should be similar; the only difference is the loaded wording of each question, so the gap reflects wording bias.

questions.stem: A student starts with the vague question, "Is the cafeteria good?" Which rewrite is a clear statistical question?
choices: Do the cafeteria's lunches taste good to Marcus, who eats in the cafeteria every day of the school year?
Does the cafeteria staff work hard each day to make lunches that every student will enjoy eating there?
How many tables and chairs are there in the cafeteria at our school at the start of the school year?
What rating, from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), do students at our school give the cafeteria's lunches?
questions.answer: What rating, from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), do students at our school give the cafeteria's lunches?
questions.solution: A good statistical question names the group (students at our school) and a measurement (a rating from 1 to 5) whose answers vary. The others ask about one person, are leading, or have a single answer.

solve.answer: What rating, from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), do students at our school give the cafeteria's lunches?
solve.work: A rating from all students at the school varies and is collectable; B is one person, C is not measurable data, D is a fixed count.

questions.stem: To find out how much students enjoy reading, a researcher asks each student how many library books they borrowed last month. What is the main weakness of this question?
choices: Borrowing counts measure use of the library, not enjoyment, and they miss books read from other sources
A count of books can never be compared between students, because every book has a different length
Students will not remember how many books they borrowed last month, so most of the answers will be missing
Enjoyment can only be measured by asking a teacher, never by asking each of the students
questions.answer: Borrowing counts measure use of the library, not enjoyment, and they miss books read from other sources
questions.solution: The measurement must match the idea being studied. Library loans are not the same as enjoying reading.

solve.answer: Borrowing counts measure use of the library, not enjoyment, and they miss books read from other sources
solve.work: Borrowing counts measure library use, not enjoyment, and miss books from other sources: a validity problem.

questions.stem: Why is a comparison group that does not use the new app (or uses the usual method) needed in a test of a new study app?
choices: It shows what scores would be like without the app, so that the two groups can be compared
It guarantees that the students who use the app will score higher than the students in the other group
It makes the sample larger, and a larger sample removes all of the bias in the way scores were measured
It lets the researcher decide which of the students will use the app and which will not use it
questions.answer: It shows what scores would be like without the app, so that the two groups can be compared
questions.solution: Without a comparison group, a rise in scores might have happened anyway. The comparison group shows what would have happened without the app.

solve.answer: It shows what scores would be like without the app, so that the two groups can be compared
solve.work: A control group shows what scores look like without the app, giving a baseline for comparison.

questions.stem: A survey was mailed to 400 randomly chosen households, and 140 households replied. What percent of the chosen households replied?
questions.solution: 140 out of 400 is 0.35, which is 35%. A low reply rate is a warning that those who replied may differ from those who did not.

questions.stem: The margin of error of a random survey is about $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for a sample of size $n$. By what factor must the sample size be multiplied to cut the margin of error in half?
questions.solution: Half of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ is $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4n}}$, so the sample must be 4 times as large.

solve.work: ME = 1/sqrt(n). Halving it requires sqrt(n) doubled, so n is multiplied by 4.

questions.stem: A principal wants to know whether students like the school's morning announcements. She surveys only the students who stay for after-school clubs. What is the main flaw in this plan?
choices: The sample is too large to be accurate, since the clubs together have a great many students in them
Students who stay for clubs cannot answer questions about the morning, because they are not at school at that time
Students in after-school clubs may differ from other students, so the sample leaves out many kinds of students
The survey should have been given in the afternoon, when students are less tired than in the morning
questions.answer: Students in after-school clubs may differ from other students, so the sample leaves out many kinds of students
questions.solution: The sample was chosen by a feature (staying for clubs) that may be related to the opinions. A random sample of all students would be better.

solve.answer: Students in after-school clubs may differ from other students, so the sample leaves out many kinds of students
solve.work: Club students may differ systematically from other students (undercoverage/selection bias). A is false: they are at school in the morning.

questions.stem: A student models drawing two aces in a row from a standard 52-card deck, without putting the first card back, by multiplying $\frac{4}{52}$ by $\frac{4}{52}$. What is the correct probability of drawing two aces in a row?
questions.solution: After one ace is drawn, 3 aces remain among 51 cards. So the probability is $\frac{4}{52}\times\frac{3}{51}=\frac{12}{2652}=\frac{1}{221}$. The student wrongly treated the draws as independent.

solve.work: Without replacement: 4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.

questions.stem: To simulate a person who succeeds with probability 0.3, a student uses random digits from 0 to 9, where 0, 1 and 2 mean success. In 40 simulated attempts there were 11 successes. What is the estimated probability of success from these 40 attempts?
questions.solution: The estimate is the relative frequency $\frac{11}{40}=0.275$. (Three of the ten digits give a model probability of 0.3, and 0.275 is close to it.)

solve.work: Estimated probability = 11/40 = 0.275.

questions.stem: In 100 rolls of a die, 1 came up 10 times, 2 came up 11 times, 3 came up 9 times, 4 came up 12 times, 5 came up 10 times and 6 came up 48 times. Which probability model fits these data best?
choices: Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has the same probability, and that probability is one sixth
The number 6 has probability 0.25 and each of the numbers 1 to 5 has probability 0.15
The number 6 has probability 0.5 and each of 1 to 5 has probability 0.1
The number 6 has probability 0.5 and each of the numbers 1 to 5 has probability 0.2
questions.answer: The number 6 has probability 0.5 and each of 1 to 5 has probability 0.1
questions.solution: The 6 came up about half the time and each other number about a tenth of the time. A model has to add to 1: $0.5+5(0.1)=1$, but $0.5+5(0.2)=1.5$.

solve.answer: The number 6 has probability 0.5 and each of 1 to 5 has probability 0.1
solve.work: Observed: 6 about 0.48, others about 0.09-0.12. D: 0.5 + 5(0.1) = 1, fits. A sums to 1.5 (invalid), B ignores the 48, C gives 6 only 0.25.

questions.stem: A random sample of 500 adults in a county was surveyed, and adults who walk daily had lower blood pressure than adults who do not. Which is the best-supported conclusion?
choices: Walking daily lowers blood pressure for adults in every county, since the sample of adults was a random one
Daily walkers in the county have lower blood pressure than the others because they walk every day
No statement about adults in the county is possible at all, since the study was not an experiment
Among adults in the county, daily walkers tend to have lower blood pressure, but walking may not be the cause
questions.answer: Among adults in the county, daily walkers tend to have lower blood pressure, but walking may not be the cause
questions.solution: The random sample lets us generalize to adults in the county. It was not an experiment, so cause is not shown.

solve.answer: Among adults in the county, daily walkers tend to have lower blood pressure, but walking may not be the cause
solve.work: Random sample lets us generalize to county adults, but it is observational, so no causal claim.

questions.stem: A random sample of 2500 people finds that 40% prefer tea to coffee. Use a margin of error of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. What is the width, in percentage points, of the interval of plausible percents for the population?
questions.solution: The margin of error is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2500}}=\frac{1}{50}=0.02$, or 2 points. The interval is 38% to 42%, whose width is 4 points.

solve.work: ME = 1/sqrt(2500) = 1/50 = 0.02 = 2 points. Interval 38% to 42%, width 4 points.

questions.stem: Method A has a mean task time of 20 minutes with a standard deviation of 6 minutes, and Method B has a mean of 22 minutes with a standard deviation of 6 minutes. Each method was tried by 15 students. A student says, "Method B is slower." What is the best statement?
choices: Method B is shown to be slower, since its mean time is larger than the mean time of Method A
Method A is shown to be faster, since it was tried by exactly the same number of students as was Method B
The 2-minute difference is small compared with the spread of about 6 minutes, so it may be due to chance
The two methods are shown to be exactly the same, since the standard deviations of both are 6
questions.answer: The 2-minute difference is small compared with the spread of about 6 minutes, so it may be due to chance
questions.solution: With a spread of 6 minutes and only 15 students per method, a 2-minute difference in means is the sort of gap chance can produce. It does not show either claim.

solve.answer: The 2-minute difference is small compared with the spread of about 6 minutes, so it may be due to chance
solve.work: Difference 2 min; SE of difference = 6 sqrt(2/15) = 2.19, so the difference is under one SE and could easily be chance.

questions.stem: For children ages 4 to 10, a fitted line is $\text{height} = 80 + 6.2\times\text{age}$, with height in centimeters and age in years. Which is the best interpretation of 6.2?
choices: A child's height increases by exactly 6.2 centimeters every year until the child reaches the age of 10
Among children aged 4 to 10, each extra year of age goes with about 6.2 cm more height on average
A newborn child, with an age of 0 years, is 6.2 centimeters tall, according to the fitted line
A child who is 6.2 years old is 80 centimeters tall, according to the fitted line given here
questions.answer: Among children aged 4 to 10, each extra year of age goes with about 6.2 cm more height on average
questions.solution: The slope is the average change in height per year of age, within the ages that were studied.

solve.answer: Among children aged 4 to 10, each extra year of age goes with about 6.2 cm more height on average
solve.work: 6.2 is the slope: each additional year of age goes with about 6.2 cm more height on average, within the 4-10 range.

questions.stem: A report finds that teens who sleep fewer hours spend more time on social media, and concludes that social media use causes teens to sleep less. What is the best critique?
choices: The report is correct, since the two quantities are related and a relation always shows the cause
Because the quantities are related, the report should say that sleep is the only thing that matters for teens
The report cannot be used, since hours of sleep and time on social media are measured in different units
The cause could run the other way, since teens who sleep less are awake longer and may use social media more
questions.answer: The cause could run the other way, since teens who sleep less are awake longer and may use social media more
questions.solution: An association does not say which way the cause runs, or whether a third factor is behind both.

solve.answer: The cause could run the other way, since teens who sleep less are awake longer and may use social media more
solve.work: Correlation does not establish direction; less sleep could lead to more social media time (reverse causation).

questions.stem: A store raised a jacket's price by 25% from 80 dollars. It now advertises "25% off!" and a customer thinks the sale price returns the jacket to 80 dollars. What is the actual sale price, in dollars?
questions.solution: After the raise the price is $80\times 1.25=100$ dollars. Taking 25% off 100 gives $100\times 0.75=75$ dollars, not 80.

questions.stem: A company shows a chart of its profit for only 3 months of the past year, the 3 best months, and says its profits are "growing steadily". What is the main concern?
choices: A chart of three months is never allowed, since every chart needs at least twelve bars in it
Profit should be written as a sentence rather than shown in a chart, so that readers can trust it
Only the best months are shown, so the chart may not represent the whole year
The months with the highest profit should be left out, since only typical months are of any interest
questions.answer: Only the best months are shown, so the chart may not represent the whole year
questions.solution: Showing only favorable data (cherry-picking) can give a false picture. All 12 months should be reported.

solve.answer: Only the best months are shown, so the chart may not represent the whole year
solve.work: Cherry-picking the 3 best months does not represent the whole year's trend.

questions.stem: A book studies 30 well-known successful entrepreneurs and finds that most took big financial risks early on. It concludes that taking big risks leads to success. What is the main concern?
choices: Thirty is too many entrepreneurs to study, since any group larger than ten people is unreliable
Taking risks is a matter of opinion, so it can never be counted or compared in any kind of study
The book should have studied only the entrepreneurs who failed, without looking at those who succeeded
Entrepreneurs who took big risks and failed are not in the study, so the risks may not lead to success
questions.answer: Entrepreneurs who took big risks and failed are not in the study, so the risks may not lead to success
questions.solution: Only the successes were studied (survivorship bias). To judge risk-taking we must also see how many risk-takers failed.

solve.answer: Entrepreneurs who took big risks and failed are not in the study, so the risks may not lead to success
solve.work: Survivorship bias: risk-takers who failed are not studied, so the conclusion is unsupported.

questions.stem: At School X, 40 of 50 students passed an exam. At School Y, 30 of 150 students passed. What percent of all 200 students passed?
questions.solution: In all, $40+30=70$ students passed out of 200, which is 35%. Averaging 80% and 20% would give 50%, which is wrong because the schools differ in size.

questions.stem: Two classes both have a mean score of 75 on a test. In Class A the scores range from 70 to 80. In Class B they range from 40 to 100. Which sentence reports the comparison best?
choices: Both classes did equally well on the test, since the mean score for each of the classes is 75
Class B did better than Class A on the test, since Class B had the highest score of any student
Class A did better than Class B on the test, since Class A had the smaller range of scores
Both classes averaged 75, but the scores in Class B varied much more than the scores in Class A
questions.answer: Both classes averaged 75, but the scores in Class B varied much more than the scores in Class A
questions.solution: A mean alone hides spread. A good report gives the center and mentions the spread.

solve.answer: Both classes averaged 75, but the scores in Class B varied much more than the scores in Class A
solve.work: Same mean but Class B is much more spread out; A reports both center and spread.

questions.stem: A report summarizes the data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 with its interquartile range. Take the lower quartile as the median of the lower four values and the upper quartile as the median of the upper four. What is the interquartile range?
questions.solution: The lower four values 2, 4, 6, 8 have median 5. The upper four values 10, 12, 14, 16 have median 13. The IQR is $13-5=8$.

questions.stem: Support for a plan rose from 40% to 50%. Which statement reports this correctly?
choices: Support rose by 10%, which is the same thing as a rise of 10 percentage points
Support rose by 10 percentage points, which is a 25% increase in support
Support rose by 25 percentage points, which is a 10% increase in support
Support rose by 10 percentage points, which is a 10% increase in support
questions.answer: Support rose by 10 percentage points, which is a 25% increase in support
questions.solution: 50% minus 40% is 10 percentage points. Relative to the starting 40%, the increase is $\frac{10}{40}=25\%$.

solve.answer: Support rose by 10 percentage points, which is a 25% increase in support
solve.work: 50 - 40 = 10 percentage points; 10/40 = 25% relative increase.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to find out whether a tutoring program helps ninth graders with math. Which version of her question is the most precise, with a clear group, a clear measurement and a clear comparison?
choices: Is the tutoring program a good program that most students in the school should join?
Do ninth graders enjoy the tutoring program more than they enjoy the other programs offered at their school?
Do ninth graders in the tutoring program score higher on the end-of-term math exam than those not in it?
How are the tutoring program and ninth graders' math knowledge related to each other in general?
questions.answer: Do ninth graders in the tutoring program score higher on the end-of-term math exam than those not in it?
questions.solution: A precise question names the group (ninth graders), the measurement (the end-of-term math exam score, compared by the average) and the two groups compared (in the program and not in the program). The other versions are vague, ask about enjoyment instead of math, or name no measurement or comparison.

solve.answer: Do ninth graders in the tutoring program score higher on the end-of-term math exam than those not in it?
solve.work: A has a clear group (ninth graders), clear measure (end-of-term math exam score) and clear comparison (in program vs not).

questions.stem: A coach wants to compare two kinds of running shoes using 20 runners, and the runners differ a lot in speed. Which plan best accounts for the differences between runners?
choices: Each runner tries both kinds on different days, with the order decided by a coin flip
Each runner chooses the pair they prefer, and the times of the two groups are compared
The first kind goes to the 10 fastest runners and the second kind to the other 10 runners
Every runner tries the first kind on day one and then the second kind on day two
questions.answer: Each runner tries both kinds on different days, with the order decided by a coin flip
questions.solution: Having every runner use both shoes removes the differences between runners, because each runner is compared with himself or herself. Deciding the order by a coin flip stops the day or the effect of practice from favoring one shoe. The other plans mix the shoes up with the runners' speed or with the order.

solve.answer: Each runner tries both kinds on different days, with the order decided by a coin flip
solve.work: Matched-pairs design: each runner is their own control, and randomizing the order removes order/day effects. B has no randomization of order; C and D are confounded with runner ability.

questions.stem: A student models the number of boys in a family of 4 children by flipping 4 fair coins, so the model gives the probabilities $\frac{1}{16}$, $\frac{4}{16}$, $\frac{6}{16}$, $\frac{4}{16}$ and $\frac{1}{16}$ for 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 boys. A survey of 100 families with 4 children found 8, 22, 38, 24 and 8 families with 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 boys. Which conclusion about the model is best?
choices: The model is poor, since no observed count is exactly equal to the expected count
The model is poor, since 38 families with 2 boys is far more than 22 families with 1 boy
The model is poor, since the observed counts add up to 100 instead of adding to 16
The model is reasonable, since each observed count is close to the count it expects
questions.answer: The model is reasonable, since each observed count is close to the count it expects
questions.solution: Out of 100 families, the model expects $6.25$, $25$, $37.5$, $25$ and $6.25$ families. The observed counts 8, 22, 38, 24 and 8 are each within a few families of these. Exact matches are not expected, because of chance variation. The model also expects more families with 2 boys than with 1 boy.

solve.answer: The model is reasonable, since each observed count is close to the count it expects
solve.work: Expected counts out of 100: 6.25, 25, 37.5, 25, 6.25. Observed 8, 22, 38, 24, 8 are all close, so the model is reasonable.

questions.stem: A model says that a fair coin flipped 100 times gives an expected 50 heads, with a standard deviation of 5 heads. A coin is flipped 100 times and gives 65 heads. How many standard deviations above the expected number is 65?
questions.solution: The difference is $65-50=15$ heads, and $\frac{15}{5}=3$ standard deviations above the expected number. A result 3 standard deviations from what a fair-coin model expects is very unlikely, so the model should be doubted.

solve.work: (65 - 50)/5 = 15/5 = 3 standard deviations.

questions.stem: A random sample of 400 voters finds that 52% support a proposal. The margin of error is about 5 percentage points. A reporter writes, "The proposal will pass." Is this justified?
choices: Yes, since 52% is more than 50%, the proposal has the support of most voters
No, support could be as low as about 47%, below 50%, so passing is not certain
Yes, since a random sample of 400 voters is large enough to be certain of the result
No, since a sample of 400 voters can say nothing at all about all of the voters
questions.answer: No, support could be as low as about 47%, below 50%, so passing is not certain
questions.solution: The sample result of 52% is only an estimate. With a margin of error of 5 points, the support among all voters could be anywhere from about 47% to 57%, so it could be below 50%, and the passing of the proposal is not certain. A random sample of this size does give useful information, but never certainty.

solve.answer: No, support could be as low as about 47%, below 50%, so passing is not certain
solve.work: 52% +/- 5 gives about 47% to 57%; values below 50% are plausible, so passing is not certain.

questions.stem: A random sample of 500 households was mailed a survey, and 120 households replied. Of the replies, 70% favored a new bus line. Which statement best reports the limitation of this result?
choices: The 70% is exactly right for all households, because the households were chosen at random
Only 24% replied, and they may differ from the rest, so the 70% may not reflect all households
The result tells us nothing, because surveys sent by mail can never be random samples
The 70% must be much too high, because nobody replied from the other 380 households
questions.answer: Only 24% replied, and they may differ from the rest, so the 70% may not reflect all households
questions.solution: The response rate is $120\div 500=24\%$. People who choose to reply may feel differently from those who do not, so the 70% may be biased even though the sample was chosen at random. It does not follow that the true value is too high or that the survey is worthless.

solve.answer: Only 24% replied, and they may differ from the rest, so the 70% may not reflect all households
solve.work: Response rate 120/500 = 24%; nonresponse bias: responders may differ, so the 70% may not reflect all households.

questions.stem: Overall, Hospital A lost 12% of its patients and Hospital B lost 8%, and a reporter concludes that Hospital B is safer. But Hospital A treats mostly patients with very serious conditions, while Hospital B treats mostly patients with minor conditions. What is the best critique?
choices: Rates of different hospitals are percents, and percents of two different hospitals can never be compared
Hospital A must be the safer hospital, because it is the one that treats the more serious cases
The difference of 4 percentage points between the two hospitals is far too small to matter
The seriousness of the cases differs between hospitals, so compare them within each level of seriousness
questions.answer: The seriousness of the cases differs between hospitals, so compare them within each level of seriousness
questions.solution: The overall rates compare hospitals whose patients are different in a way that strongly affects the outcome. A fair comparison looks at patients with similar conditions in each hospital. The other critiques are wrong: percents can be compared, and nothing shows that Hospital A is safer.

solve.answer: The seriousness of the cases differs between hospitals, so compare them within each level of seriousness
solve.work: Case severity is a confounder (Simpson's paradox risk): compare death rates within each severity level.

questions.stem: A headline says, "Risk doubles!" because the number of cases of a rare condition rose from 2 in every 10000 people to 4 in every 10000 people. By how many percentage points did the risk rise?
questions.solution: The risk rose from $\frac{2}{10000}=0.02\%$ to $\frac{4}{10000}=0.04\%$, a rise of $0.04-0.02=0.02$ percentage points. "Doubles" is true in relative terms, but the actual rise is tiny and the headline makes it sound large.

questions.stem: A student finds that the correlation between hours studied and test score for 40 students is $r=0.82$. Which sentence is the best way to report this?
choices: Hours and scores of these 40 students have a strong positive linear association, which alone does not show cause.
Studying more hours causes higher scores, because the correlation of 0.82 is strong and positive.
Hours and scores of these 40 students are strongly associated, and hours explains 82% of the variation.
Because $r=0.82$, 82% of these 40 students scored higher when they studied more hours.
questions.answer: Hours and scores of these 40 students have a strong positive linear association, which alone does not show cause.
questions.solution: A good report names the variables, the direction and strength, the group, and the limit on the conclusion: correlation alone does not show cause. The value $r=0.82$ is not a percent of students, and the share of the variation explained is $r^2\approx 0.67$, not 0.82.

solve.answer: Hours and scores of these 40 students have a strong positive linear association, which alone does not show cause.
solve.work: r = 0.82 is a strong positive linear association for these 40 students; correlation alone does not show causation. r^2 = 0.67, not 0.82, so C is wrong; B claims cause; D misreads r.

questions.stem: A report combines two groups. Group A has 40 students with a mean score of 80, and group B has 60 students with a mean score of 70. What mean score should the report give for all 100 students?
questions.solution: Weight each group by its size. The total of the scores is $40\times 80+60\times 70=3200+4200=7400$. The mean for all 100 students is $7400\div 100=74$, not $\frac{80+70}{2}=75$.

questions.stem: A researcher asks, "Does sleep affect performance on tests?" She must decide how to measure each idea. Which pair of measures is the most clearly defined?
choices: How rested a student says that he or she feels, and how smart the student seems to the teacher during class
Whether the student went to bed early or late, and whether the student did well or badly at school this year in general
Hours slept the previous night, reported in whole hours, and the score out of 100 on a math quiz given the next morning
Hours slept during a whole week, and how the student feels about taking tests in general, rated by a parent
questions.answer: Hours slept the previous night, reported in whole hours, and the score out of 100 on a math quiz given the next morning
questions.solution: Each idea needs a measurement that anyone could repeat. Hours slept and a quiz score are numbers; the other pairs are vague or measure something different.

solve.answer: Hours slept the previous night, reported in whole hours, and the score out of 100 on a math quiz given the next morning
solve.work: B gives precise, measurable definitions: hours slept the night before (whole hours) and a score out of 100 the next morning.

questions.stem: A survey asks, "How often do you skip breakfast?" with the options Never, Rarely, Sometimes and Often. What is the main weakness of the options?
choices: There are fewer than ten options, so the data cannot be summarized into counts of each answer
The options go in order from least to most, which forces every student to choose the middle one
Words cannot be counted, so no summary of the answers is possible with options like these ones
The words are not defined, so two students with the same habit might choose different answers
questions.answer: The words are not defined, so two students with the same habit might choose different answers
questions.solution: "Rarely" and "Sometimes" mean different things to different students. Clear ranges, such as 0 days, 1 to 2 days, and so on, would fix this. Word answers can still be counted.

solve.answer: The words are not defined, so two students with the same habit might choose different answers
solve.work: Never/Rarely/Sometimes/Often are vague; the same habit could be labelled differently by different students.

questions.stem: Which research question could be investigated with a randomized experiment, rather than only with an observational study?
choices: Do students who were born in the summer have a different average height than students who were born in the winter?
Does listening to quiet music while solving puzzles change the number of puzzles that students solve in 20 minutes?
Do students who have older brothers or sisters read more books per year than students who do not have any?
Do students who live far from school get a different amount of sleep than students who live close to the school?
questions.answer: Does listening to quiet music while solving puzzles change the number of puzzles that students solve in 20 minutes?
questions.solution: An experiment needs the researcher to assign the treatment. Music can be assigned at random; birth season, siblings and distance from school cannot.

solve.answer: Does listening to quiet music while solving puzzles change the number of puzzles that students solve in 20 minutes?
solve.work: Birth season, distance from school and siblings cannot be assigned. Music while solving puzzles can be randomly assigned: D.

questions.stem: A farmer wants to compare two seed types. The north half of her field is wetter than the south half. Which plan best accounts for the difference between the halves?
choices: Plant the first seed type in the whole north half of the field and the second seed type in the whole south half
Divide each half into equal plots and use a coin flip to give each seed type to half of the plots in each half
Plant each seed type in the part of the field where she expects it to grow best, using past seasons as a guide
Plant both seed types in the south half only, since the wetter north half would unfairly favor one of the types
questions.answer: Divide each half into equal plots and use a coin flip to give each seed type to half of the plots in each half
questions.solution: Blocking: because wetness differs, each seed type is tried on both the wet and the dry half, assigned at random within each half. Then wetness cannot explain a difference.

solve.answer: Divide each half into equal plots and use a coin flip to give each seed type to half of the plots in each half
solve.work: Blocking by wetness with random assignment within each block (D) accounts for the difference; C confounds seed with wetness.

questions.stem: A random survey of 100 people has a margin of error of about 0.1, using the rule that the margin of error is about $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. About how many people are needed for a margin of error of 0.02?
questions.solution: We need $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}=0.02$, so $\sqrt{n}=50$ and $n=2500$.

solve.work: 1/sqrt(n) = 0.02 gives sqrt(n) = 50, n = 2500. (Check: n=100 gives 0.1.)

questions.stem: In a trial of a new pill for headaches, patients are randomly given the pill or a look-alike placebo. The doctor who rates each patient's pain afterward knows which patients received the pill. What is the concern and the best fix?
choices: The patients should be told which pill they have, so that the ratings of the doctor will be more honest
The placebo should be removed, so that every patient receives the same real pill and the two groups are equal
The doctor should give the pill to the patients who have the worst pain, in order to make the test fair
The doctor's knowledge could affect the ratings, so the doctor who rates the pain should not know who got which pill
questions.answer: The doctor's knowledge could affect the ratings, so the doctor who rates the pain should not know who got which pill
questions.solution: A rater who knows the group may, without meaning to, rate one group differently. Keeping the rater unaware (blinding) removes that bias.

solve.answer: The doctor's knowledge could affect the ratings, so the doctor who rates the pain should not know who got which pill
solve.work: The rater's knowledge could bias the ratings; blind the rater (double-blind).

questions.stem: A poll calls landline numbers from a directory on weekday mornings and asks about support for a new tax. Which statement best describes the main weakness of the poll?
choices: Calling by phone cannot be used to collect opinions, since opinions can only be collected in person
Landline users always support a new tax, so the percent who support it must be reported as too high
The directory has too many numbers on it, and a very long list always causes random errors in a poll
People who work during the day or have only cell phones are less likely to be reached, so they are under-represented
questions.answer: People who work during the day or have only cell phones are less likely to be reached, so they are under-represented
questions.solution: The people who can be reached by this plan differ from the whole population, so the sample is biased (undercoverage). Calling at other times and including cell phones would help.

solve.answer: People who work during the day or have only cell phones are less likely to be reached, so they are under-represented
solve.work: Weekday-morning landline calls miss daytime workers and cell-only households: undercoverage.

questions.stem: A game's model says a player wins 3 dollars with probability 0.2 and loses 1 dollar with probability 0.8. What is the expected gain per game, in dollars?
questions.solution: Expected gain $=3(0.2)-1(0.8)=0.6-0.8=-0.2$ dollars. On average the player loses 0.2 dollars per game.

questions.stem: A model says each of 3 students passes a test with probability 0.6, independently of the others. What is the probability that at least one of the three students does not pass?
questions.solution: All three pass with probability $0.6^3=0.216$. At least one does not pass is the opposite, so $1-0.216=0.784$.

solve.work: P(all pass) = 0.6^3 = 0.216; at least one fails = 1 - 0.216 = 0.784.

questions.stem: A model says a spinner has 4 equally likely sections: red, blue, green and yellow. In 200 spins, a simulation of the model shows that the number of reds falls between 36 and 64 in 95% of repeated runs. A real spinner gives 62 reds in 200 spins. What is the best conclusion?
choices: 62 reds is more than the 50 that the model expects, so the model has been shown to be wrong by the real spinner
62 reds is within the range that the model usually produces, so there is no strong evidence against the model
The model is proven correct, since 62 reds is within the range that the repeated simulations usually gave
The model must be wrong, because the real spinner would then need to give exactly 50 reds in 200 spins
questions.answer: 62 reds is within the range that the model usually produces, so there is no strong evidence against the model
questions.solution: The model expects 50 reds, but results from 36 to 64 are typical. 62 is typical, so it does not contradict the model (and one result cannot prove a model correct).

solve.answer: 62 reds is within the range that the model usually produces, so there is no strong evidence against the model
solve.work: 62 is inside the 95% range 36-64, so the data are consistent with the model; not proof, but no strong evidence against it.

questions.stem: A shop's model says the number of customers arriving in an hour is equally likely to be any whole number from 0 to 10. In 200 recorded hours, 4, 5 or 6 customers arrived in 130 of the hours, and 0 or 10 customers arrived in only 6 of the hours. What does this suggest?
choices: The model fits well, because averages near the middle are always found in real data for every shop
The data must be wrong, since a shop cannot have 130 hours with 4, 5 or 6 customers arriving in them
The equally likely assumption does not fit; a model with more probability near the middle would fit better
The model should be changed so that 0 customers and 10 customers become the most likely numbers of customers of all
questions.answer: The equally likely assumption does not fit; a model with more probability near the middle would fit better
questions.solution: An equally likely model predicts about $\frac{3}{11}\times 200\approx 55$ hours with 4, 5 or 6 customers and about 36 hours with 0 or 10. The data show 130 and 6, so the middle values are far more likely than the model says.

solve.answer: The equally likely assumption does not fit; a model with more probability near the middle would fit better
solve.work: Uniform model expects 3/11 x 200 = 54.5 hours with 4-6 customers (observed 130) and 2/11 x 200 = 36.4 with 0 or 10 (observed 6). Uniform fails; a model peaked in the middle fits better.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment with 10,000 students, those who used a tutoring app scored a mean of 0.3 points higher on a 100-point test than those who did not, a difference too large to be due to chance. Which statement is best?
choices: The app made no difference, since a gain of 0.3 points is less than a gain of 1 point in the score
The app raised scores a great deal, since a difference of this size is too large to be due to chance
The app probably did raise scores, but the effect is so small that it may not matter in practice
The result is not trustworthy, since an experiment with 10,000 students is too large to be reliable
questions.answer: The app probably did raise scores, but the effect is so small that it may not matter in practice
questions.solution: With very large samples, even a tiny difference can be statistically clear. A 0.3-point gain out of 100 is real but of little practical importance.

solve.answer: The app probably did raise scores, but the effect is so small that it may not matter in practice
solve.work: Statistically significant but 0.3 of 100 points is tiny: real but practically unimportant.

questions.stem: A line fitted to the number of words that toddlers know at ages 12 to 24 months is $\text{words} = 10\times\text{age}-100$ (age in months). A student uses it to predict the words known at 6 months and gets $-40$. What is the main problem?
choices: A line cannot be used to predict any value, since lines can only describe the data that are already known
6 months is outside the ages of 12 to 24 months used to fit the line, so the prediction is not reliable
A line cannot be used to predict words, which must be counted instead of being measured
The prediction should have been rounded to the nearest ten words, which would have changed it to $-40$
questions.answer: 6 months is outside the ages of 12 to 24 months used to fit the line, so the prediction is not reliable
questions.solution: Predicting outside the range of the data (extrapolation) is unreliable, and here it gives a negative number of words, which is impossible.

solve.answer: 6 months is outside the ages of 12 to 24 months used to fit the line, so the prediction is not reliable
solve.work: 10(6) - 100 = -40, impossible; 6 months is outside the 12-24 month data range (extrapolation).

questions.stem: A random sample of 400 voters finds that 46% support a proposal. Use a margin of error of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. By how many percentage points does the top of the interval of plausible percents extend above 50%?
questions.solution: The margin of error is $\frac{1}{20}=0.05$, or 5 points. The interval is 41% to 51%, so it extends 1 point above 50%. A majority is therefore still plausible.

solve.work: ME = 1/sqrt(400) = 1/20 = 5 points. Interval 41% to 51%; the top is 1 point above 50%.

questions.stem: A random sample of 300 students at one school finds that 45% of them walk to school. Which statement is NOT supported by this result?
choices: Exactly 45% of all of the students at the school walk to school
A different random sample of 300 students might give a percent a little different from 45%
The percent of all students at the school who walk is probably near 45% according to the sample
The result describes this school and cannot be applied to every school in the state
questions.answer: Exactly 45% of all of the students at the school walk to school
questions.solution: A sample gives an estimate, not the exact value, for the population. The other statements are fair readings of the result.

solve.answer: Exactly 45% of all of the students at the school walk to school
solve.work: A, B, C are reasonable statements about sampling variability and scope. D claims an exact population value, which a sample cannot establish.

questions.stem: A test finds every person who has a condition, and it also gives a positive result for 5% of the people who do not have the condition. Among 1000 people, 2% have the condition. How many of the people who test positive do not have the condition?
questions.solution: 20 people have the condition and 980 do not. 5% of 980 is 49 false positives. So of the 69 positive results, 49 are false.

solve.work: 20 have the condition, 980 do not. False positives = 5% of 980 = 49.

questions.stem: A researcher compares 20 unrelated foods with a health outcome and reports the one food that showed an association that would happen by chance only 5% of the time. What is the best critique?
choices: A food can only be compared with one health outcome, so the other comparisons should be removed
A result that would happen by chance 5% of the time proves that the food causes the outcome
With 20 comparisons, about one association is expected by chance alone, so a single result proves little
Twenty comparisons is too few, since a study needs at least a hundred comparisons before any can count
questions.answer: With 20 comparisons, about one association is expected by chance alone, so a single result proves little
questions.solution: At the 5% level, about $20\times 0.05=1$ false association is expected among 20 tests of unrelated foods.

solve.answer: With 20 comparisons, about one association is expected by chance alone, so a single result proves little
solve.work: Multiple comparisons: with 20 tests at 5%, about 1 false positive is expected by chance.

questions.stem: An ad says a drug "cuts the risk of a heart attack by 50%." Without the drug, the risk is 4 in every 1000 people. Among 10,000 people who take the drug instead of not taking it, how many fewer heart attacks are expected?
questions.solution: Without the drug, $\frac{4}{1000}\times 10000=40$ heart attacks. The drug halves that to 20, so 20 fewer. The "50%" sounds large, but the risk fell by only 0.2 percentage points.

solve.work: Without drug: 4/1000 x 10000 = 40. With 50% cut: 20. 40 - 20 = 20 fewer.

questions.stem: Across 40 regions, those with more chess clubs per person have higher average math scores. A writer says that joining a chess club raises a child's math score. What is the main concern?
choices: Data about regions do not show what happens to individual children, who may differ from their region's average
Forty regions are too many to compare, since a comparison must use only two regions to be fair
Average scores cannot be calculated for a whole region, but only for single children one at a time
Chess clubs and math are different subjects, so a study can never relate one of them to the other one
questions.answer: Data about regions do not show what happens to individual children, who may differ from their region's average
questions.solution: A pattern among group averages need not hold for individuals (the ecological fallacy), and it does not show cause either.

solve.answer: Data about regions do not show what happens to individual children, who may differ from their region's average
solve.work: Ecological fallacy: region-level association does not show individual effect (also not causal).

questions.stem: A report says the mean of 8 test scores is 76. After a ninth score is added, the report says the mean is 78. What is the ninth score?
questions.solution: The total of the first 8 scores is $76\times 8=608$. The total of 9 scores is $78\times 9=702$. The ninth score is $702-608=94$.

questions.stem: For 50 adults, a student finds that the correlation between weekly hours of exercise and resting heart rate is $r=-0.8$, so $r^2=0.64$. Which sentence is the best report?
choices: About 64% of the variation in these adults' resting heart rates is accounted for by the linear fit with exercise hours
Exercise lowers resting heart rate by 64%, according to the correlation of these 50 adults between the two
64% of the adults had a lower resting heart rate when they exercised more, as the correlation of these adults shows
About 80% of the variation in these adults' resting heart rates is accounted for by the linear fit with exercise hours
questions.answer: About 64% of the variation in these adults' resting heart rates is accounted for by the linear fit with exercise hours
questions.solution: $r^2$ is the fraction of the variation in one variable accounted for by a linear relationship with the other. It does not show cause, and it is not a percent of people.

solve.answer: About 64% of the variation in these adults' resting heart rates is accounted for by the linear fit with exercise hours
solve.work: r^2 = 0.64 is the fraction of variation in heart rate explained by the linear relationship with exercise hours.

questions.stem: Which information should a report include so that others could repeat the investigation?
choices: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and how each variable was measured
Only the final conclusion of the investigation, stated in as few words as possible and with no details
Only a graph of the results, without any description of the way in which the data were obtained
The names of the people who took part, so that other researchers can ask each of them the same questions
questions.answer: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and how each variable was measured
questions.solution: To repeat a study, others need the sampling method, the sample size and the measurements used.

solve.answer: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and how each variable was measured
solve.work: Replication needs sampling method, sample size and measurement of variables; names would breach privacy.

questions.stem: A data set of home prices is skewed to the right, with a few very expensive homes. Which pair of statistics should a report use to describe the center and the spread?
choices: The mean and the standard deviation, since they use every value and so they are always the best choice
The median and the interquartile range, since they are not pulled by the few very high prices
The mode and the range, since the range is the least affected by the few very expensive homes
The mean and the mode, since together they show how far apart the high and low prices are
questions.answer: The median and the interquartile range, since they are not pulled by the few very high prices
questions.solution: For skewed data with outliers, the median and IQR describe the typical home and the middle spread, and are not pulled by the extreme prices.

solve.answer: The median and the interquartile range, since they are not pulled by the few very high prices
solve.work: For right-skewed data, the median and IQR are resistant to the extreme values.
